articles.title_orig: Beijing’s new “common language” law doesn’t sound so common
articles.title_zh: Beijing’s new “common language” law doesn’t sound so common
articles.content_orig:
Uyghur students study Mandarin beneath a portrait of Mao Zedong at a school in Hetian, Xinjiang, in 2006. China’s push to make Mandarin the nation’s sole language rests on an old Marxist premise – that minority cultures sit a rung lower on a ladder toward “civilisation” (Photo by Servais Mont/Getty Images)
China’s bid for one national language rests on an old idea – that some cultures remain less developed – and coincides with a push for global status.

Beijing’s new “common language” law doesn’t sound so common
For more than a century, China’s governments have sought one official language understood by everyone, used in public business, conducive to the sense that their population shares the sort of political identity associated with a “nation”. Late Qing constitutional reforms made Mandarin (Opens in new window) the “national language”. The 1911 revolution brought new leaders hoping to “circulate Mandarin Chinese … all over the Republic of China”. Mao Zedong, in power after 1949, accelerated centralisation (Opens in new window) . His program merged spreading Mandarin with simplifying characters and working ideological meanings into them.
In 1994, China’s state mandated Mandarin proficiency tests for teachers, broadcasters, and actors and launched a campaign (Opens in new window) to link “speaking Mandarin with being educated and cultured.”
Still, in 2014, one-third (Opens in new window) of China’s population could not read Mandarin.
Learning “Chinese” as a language is a heterogenous bucket. 150 dialects or languages were spoken in the province of Yunnan alone in 2009 (Opens in new window) . Some 45% (Opens in new window) of China’s far northwestern region Xinjiang speaks Uyghur.
Global power starts with internal unity, seems to be the argument.
Rule of law is a vague idea in China, and sometimes it takes only a new sense of what is politically popular, not what is legal, to push language restrictions. Without explaining the rationale, public security bureaus have imprisoned or surveilled (Opens in new window) teachers advocating Tibetan in schools and removed (Opens in new window) songs with phrases like “I am a Mongolian” from online venues.
However, laws institutionalise campaigns, reduce recourse, and signal state priorities – with two new ones coming into effect in 2026.
A language law (Opens in new window) in January aims for a sense of “Chinese nation,” along with “cultural confidence” on the world stage. It shifts non-Mandarin language use in schools from the language of instruction to a one-off independent language course and mandates Mandarin teaching starting in preschool (Opens in new window) . Radio, film, television, video games, public signs, print publications, and newly printed textbooks must also use Mandarin (Opens in new window) .
There used to be exceptions for ethnic minorities. But a March 2026 law revised (Opens in new window) China’s ethnicity policy, declaring (Opens in new window) non-Mandarin language instruction “no longer necessary”. That change came with other efforts at absorbing the 9% of China’s population not registered as Han into the Han population: housing policies that facilitate ethnic mixing, for example.
Why starts with ideology. No matter how far China has gone towards “capitalism with Chinese characteristics”, its state remains a Marxist institution. Between 1992 and 2007, 27 universities added (Opens in new window) schools of Marxism.
How is Marx related to language policy? Marx prescribed an inevitable historical evolution from “primitive” society through feudalism, capitalism, eventually to communist society; each had greater technological capacity and different labour relations. This view of historical “progress” persists among China’s leaders, who shifted (Opens in new window) elementary-school textbooks in 2022 to promote a story of Chinese “civilisation” evolving from “primitive society” in the “prehistoric period.”
This view maps onto a state-driven sense that ethnicity pairs with “degree of primitiveness”. Tourists come to Wengding Village (Opens in new window) because it is “the last primitive tribe in China.” The People’s Daily celebrates (Opens in new window) the spread of Internet to “the Dulong people,” whose “isolated” location has prevented evolution from a “primitive … lifestyle”. When someone sped by on the road in Qinghai, my taxi driver told me it was probably one of the area’s Tibetans, who tended to be backwards. So ethnicity goes with degree of primitiveness in China, and primitiveness goes with where you are on the progression towards communist “civilisation”. In this context, the March 2026 ethnicity law (Opens in new window) was not only on “Promoting Ethnic Unity” but also on “Promoting Progress.”
China’s been en route to Communism since 1949. So why now? Sometimes states tighten language policies during periods of international expansion. Defunct with the French Revolution, the Academie Française returned with Napoleon, as he reached for Europe. As the Soviet Union spread into imperial Russia’s old periphery, it sought to integrate central Asian and eastern European subjects in part through co-opt-and-conquer language policies. Efforts to “standardise the Japanese language” in the mid-to-late 1800s accompanied (Opens in new window) annexation of Korea and Taiwan.
Certainly, China’s language policies respond in part to domestic worries (Opens in new window) that difference could make a case for separation. As one of my Chinese classmates informed me in 2024, religion in Xinjiang isn’t spiritual; it’s being used for separatism. By 2020 (Opens in new window) , in Inner Mongolia, not using Mongolian in school was a “political duty.” In 2019, Xi Jinping felt the need to tell (Opens in new window) Nepal’s prime minister that “anyone attempting to create division in any region of China will only end up with pulverized bodies and crushed bones”.
But tightened language policy also parallels widened aims abroad. China’s state places language policy in the context of “Cold War” dynamics, a phrase that only emerged (Opens in new window) to imply US–China relations at the 18th and 19th Party congresses in 2012 and 2017 (Opens in new window) . Mandating Mandarin use in schools, broadcasts, publications, and other domains fights (Opens in new window) “servile imitation of foreign models,” this argument goes. China pushed towards the Global South with the Belt and Road Initiative around the same time (2013 onwards). Thus, language homogenisation has come along with an effort by China’s state to elevate itself (in the Soviet Union’s image) to the status of a global pole in a bipolar world. Global power starts with internal unity, seems to be the argument.
How long that logic holds is a separate question. The Soviet Union went through similar policies, and native-language literature movements (Opens in new window) responded to them in the 1970s and 1980s. Will China’s policies bend language to politics, or will it be the other way around?
Sophia Charles is a graduate student with long-term interests in nationality-related topics, grassroots politics, and social organisation in modern China and Soviet Russia. She graduated in 2024 from Harvard, where she studied History and Physics, along with learning Chinese and Russian.

articles.title_orig: Apple CEO Presses Software Chief to Pursue More Ambitious AI Strategy
articles.title_zh: Apple CEO Presses Software Chief to Pursue More Ambitious AI Strategy
articles.content_orig:
Dave Wehner, Meta's chief strategy officer, is leaving the company for four-year-old AI startup Fireworks.
At Fireworks — an AI inference and model-training platform focused on open models that was valued at $17.5 billion during a Series D fundraising round in July — Wehner will assume the CFO role, he announced on X on Friday.
Wehner will be tasked with scaling the company's finances and operations, Fireworks CEO Lin Qiao said in a statement to CNBC.
"Fireworks has the right mission for the moment," Wehner wrote on X, adding: "I've become increasingly bullish on what they are building. There's a remarkable depth of technical talent here, coupled with a very practical focus on what customers need."
The AI startup, founded in 2022 by former Meta and Google employees, is a platform that lets developers customize and run open models for their businesses. Its latest investment round was led by Atreides Management, Index Ventures and TCV, but Fireworks is also backed by Nvidia and Sequoia Capital. Business Insider reported that it is in early talks to raise funds again at a possible $30 billion to $40 billion valuation.
Wehner joined Meta, then called Facebook, in 2012 and was the company's chief financial officer from 2014 to 2022.
"Dave helped guide Meta through tremendous growth and complexity over 14 years, and brought disciplined thinking to some of our hardest company-level decisions," Meta COO Javier Olivan said in a statement to CNBC.
Fireworks is notably smaller than Meta — the tech giant has about a $1.56 trillion market capitalization as of Friday's close — and its competitors, which include OpenAI and Anthropic.
"Dave told me he wanted to get back to a smaller company where he could build toward a big impact again," Fireworks' Lin wrote in a LinkedIn post on Friday. "He sees AI as the defining technology shift of his lifetime and wants to help shape what comes next."
The company's size has not made it immune to the risks and complications often associated with AI technology. In October, the company found "a security incident involving unauthorized use of internal Fireworks credentials," in which "an unauthorized third party accessed environment variables used in evaluation jobs in a limited number of customer accounts," it said in a press release.
"Based on our investigation at this time, we have not detected evidence of unauthorized access to customer models, datasets, training data, personal information, or inference traffic within the Fireworks security perimeter or control," the release said.

articles.title_orig: Train collision in Egypt kills 4, injures 88
articles.title_zh: Train collision in Egypt kills 4, injures 88
articles.content_orig:
Egypt’s 110 million people depend heavily on rail transport, but the network has suffered repeated deadly accidents
Two trains collided south of the Egyptian capital on Sunday, derailing several carriages, killing four and injuring dozens, according to the authorities.
Egypt’s railway authority said a train travelling from Giza to Fayoum crashed into the rear of another service heading south from Cairo to the city of Aswan.
The health ministry said an initial count put the toll from the crash at four passengers killed, with 88 others currently being treated for injuries in hospitals around the Giza area.

articles.title_orig: A ‘Chaotic Race’ for the World’s Top Diplomat
articles.title_zh: A ‘Chaotic Race’ for the World’s Top Diplomat
articles.content_orig:
Rebeca Grynspan of Costa Rica extended her lead in the race for United Nations secretary-general in yet another informal ballot held by the Security Council. The two new candidates that joined the contest recently struggled to get the minimum of nine “encourage” votes.
In the straw poll on Thursday, Nov. 5, Grynspan got 12 encourage ballots, one higher than the last straw poll, on Oct. 30, according to multiple leaked results seen by PassBlue. The number of “discourage” votes for her also dropped to three, but she needs to get zero discourage, including no veto, for the Council recommend her as the nominee to the General Assembly.
In Thursday’s undifferentiated straw poll, it is unclear which Council members cast a discourage vote against Grynspan, though there is plenty of speculation that it has consistently been the US throughout the series of informal balloting and possibly Russia this time — both veto holders. A color-coded ballot reveals vetos from a permanent member (Britain, China and France as well), but not who cast them.
No date has been set for another straw poll or whether it will be color-coded. (The only such poll in the race so far was held on Oct. 16.)
Lana Nusseibeh , a candidate from the United Arab Emirates (who was born in 1978), and Feridun Sinirlioglu , 70, of Türkiye, are the newest entrants in the race. From the start of her nomination, announced on Oct. 21, Nusseibeh has been facing strong pushback from civil society groups as the media also scrutinize her country’s enabling role in the war in Sudan and its related atrocities.
The New York Times reported on Nov. 5 that UN investigators had linked an Emirati security company to the country’s ruling family to deploy Colombian mercenaries alongside the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), the paramilitary group fighting the Sudanese Armed Forces in Sudan’s civil war. Nusseibeh, who until recently was a top UAE diplomat, has over the years repeatedly denied Emirati support of the RSF.
Soon after she announced her candidacy as UN secretary-general, Human Rights Watch questioned whether she would defend the independence of UN investigative bodies examining her government’s actions in Sudan and elsewhere.
The UAE authorities also repeatedly reject allegations that they support either side in Sudan’s war, despite numerous UN independent inquiries and other expert institutions saying otherwise. That includes a Human Rights Council’s fact-finding mission report published in September, saying the UAE has “played a significant role in networks involved in the recruitment, financing, transportation and deployment” of foreign military contractors and the provision of military-related support benefiting the RSF.
Nusseibeh is saying in her campaign that ending the conflict will be a priority if she is selected UN chief. But human rights experts say that even if she commissioned an independent UN inquiry into the Sudan war, as the head of the UN, it could be challenging for her to separate such a step from her country’s own geopolitical ambitions.
Sinirlioglu announced his candidacy on Oct. 30. He is a former foreign minister, UN ambassador and currently the secretary-general of the Organization for the Security and Cooperation in Europe. In Thursday’s straw poll, he received three encourage, eight discourage and four “no opinion” votes, far below the threshold to be a viable contender. Like another candidate in the race, Olara Otunnu of Uganda, the Turk was included in the Council’s informal ballot before he met with the General Assembly, a formality in which the other nominees have participated.
The public dialogue for Sinirlioglu is scheduled for Nov. 6, and an informal, private meeting with Council members is planned for Nov. 9.
An outside expert on the UN race told PassBlue that China may be insisting for now that the informal polling remain undifferentiated rather than color-coded to give more time to candidates from the Latin American region — of which there are five — to drum up more support while Beijing continues to assess Nusseibeh.
In May, China’s representative at the UN told reporters that his country preferred that a woman — without specifying who — should clinch the top UN post and that the selection process should abide by the UN’s regional rotation system. (The UN has never been led by a woman, and the Latin American-Caribbean area says it’s their turn for the job.)
In Thursday’s poll, Rafael Grossi of Argentina remained second, with nine encourage, four discourage and two no opinions, reflecting no change from the Oct. 30 balloting. Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett of Guyana also retained her same spot from the last poll, with eight encourage, but her discourage numbers fell to five from six and she drew two no opinions, one more than last time.
Otunnu got four encourage, nine discourage and two no opinions. María Fernanda Espinosa, backed by Antigua and Barbuda but an Ecuadorian, received three encourage, 10 discourage and two no opinion. The results of the Tonga-nominated Ivonne A-Baki (also Ecuadorian) remained unchanged: One encourage and 14 discourage.
The second term of Secretary-General António Guterres ends on Dec. 31.
Damilola Banjo is an award-winning staff reporter for PassBlue who has covered a wide range of topics, from Africa-centered stories to gender equality to UN peacekeeping and US-UN relations. She also oversees all video production for PassBlue. She was a Dag Hammarskjold fellow in 2023 and a Pulitzer Center postgraduate fellow in 2021. She was part of the BBC Africa team that produced the Emmy-nominated documentary, "Sex for Grades." In addition, she worked for WFAE, an NPR affiliate in Charlotte, N.C. Banjo has a master's of science degree from the Columbia University Graduate School of Journalism and an undergraduate degree from the University of Ibadan in Nigeria.
We would love your thoughts. Please comment:
The race for the next Secretary General is now a competition between candidates over who can be the most anodyne.  Venality and the collective abrogation of responsibility by the leaders of the P-5 and by the many and varied sheep in the General Assembly has brought us here.  Not even the stalwart supporters of the UN system have risen to its defence and insisted on better.  Not a peep from the Nordics.  Utter silence from Canada.  Acquiescence from South Africa.  The list goes on…
But it gets worse. Fully 7 members of the Security Council judge Ms. Nussebeih of the UAE to be a suitable candidate for UN Secretary General even though, on the evidence, she is just about the closest one can get in international relations to being an adjudicated liar.  Is this a firm foundation for the highest level of diplomacy?
These are shameful days for the purported stewards of the Westphalian state system.  Historians in every language will look back in amazement on these times.  And they will surely ask, “How could they have been so stupid?”.
Thank you again Damilola/Pass Blue. Easily the best reporting on the UNSG race.

articles.title_orig: Europe will be represented in Abu Dhabi talks on Ukraine, French foreign minister says
articles.title_zh: Europe will be represented in Abu Dhabi talks on Ukraine, French foreign minister says
articles.content_orig:
Paris and Europe will have a seat at the table in next week’s U.S.-brokered peace talks between Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said on Sunday.
France “will be around the table,” Barrot told French radio RTL . “The Europeans will be well represented and France will be in Abu Dhabi to participate in these discussions. I cannot yet tell you who will represent France on this occasion, but it will certainly be there.”
U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff announced last Monday there would be trilateral talks between Washington, Kyiv and Moscow on Nov. 10–11, the first since a summit in February. But the extent to which Europe will take part in the talks remains unclear.
“In recent weeks, Europeans have made their voices heard, expressing to the American mediator that no discussion concerning the future of the continent can disregard our expectations and demands,” Barrot told RTL.
European Commission spokesperson Paula Pinho said Friday the EU executive didn’t yet have details to share, but added that “it’s obviously up to the European Union to decide on matters which affect its security and on matters which are of its competence.”
The EU has scrambled to agree on who should represent it at the peace talks and who, if anyone, should be in contact with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni urged European Council President António Costa to settle the issue in a letter this week, prompting Costa to put it on the agenda of the Nov. 13 leaders’ summit. Meloni’s letter was partly prompted by a phone call Finland’s Alexander Stubb and Norway’s Jonas Gahr Støre made to Putin on Oct. 27, which took some European leaders by surprise.
Meanwhile, the European Commission hosted talks on Ukraine’s reconstruction on Wednesday, bringing together representatives from Ukraine, the U.S., U.K., Germany, France, NATO and the World Bank.
U.S. President Donald Trump spoke late Thursday of a “big, beautiful agreement,” after meeting with Putin’s envoy Kirill Dmitriev, adding: “It’s going to involve more than Ukraine, and I could even say it might involve all of Europe.” The plan has brought anxiety among EU officials, who fear it risks sidelining the continent and emboldening Putin.
“We already have a European security architecture in place — NATO and European Union both have their respective roles,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Friday in response to the U.S. plan. “We must make sure Ukraine is integrated into this architecture. The problem remains that Russia keeps breaking the treaties that underpin it … Putin does not have a veto over European security.”

articles.title_orig: Poppi founders are going after PepsiCo's Gatorade with new beverage startup Jetty
articles.title_zh: Poppi founders are going after PepsiCo's Gatorade with new beverage startup Jetty
articles.content_orig:
After disrupting the soda category with Poppi, founders Allison and Stephen Ellsworth are now taking aim at hydration with their new brand, Jetty.
Starting Monday, Jetty drinks and ready-to-mix electrolyte packets will be on shelves at Whole Foods grocery stores and available online at Target and Amazon .
The new, self-funded venture directly pits the Ellsworths against PepsiCo , which bought Poppi for $1.95 billion in 2025. Pepsi owns Gatorade, which dominates the U.S. sports drink category with about 60% market share, according to Numerator data.
Poppi shook up the soda category with prebiotic fiber, low calorie and sugar counts and its fun marketing aimed at Generation Z and millennials. Jetty looks to upend the hydration category through a similar strategy. To do so, it will face off not only against Gatorade but also a swarm of other upstarts looking to get in on the electrolyte-fueled trend.
For decades, Gatorade and other sports drinks have pitched their products to athletes who need electrolytes and fluids after an intense workout, although many consumers drink them every day without even sweating. Jetty is aimed at people who need a hydration boost, but not the same level of electrolytes or sugar as a traditional sports drink.
"No one has really created a product for just everyday hydration — literally everyday hydration for normal people," Allison Ellsworth, Jetty's chief brand officer, told CNBC. "Like I woke up this morning, I didn't run a marathon."
Following Poppi's sale to PepsiCo, Ellsworth stayed on as an advisor to the brand, although she said she is no longer involved in the day-to-day operations.
After 10 years building Poppi, Ellsworth said, she finally had free time. As Ellsworth tells it, she went to the doctor for the first time in a decade. She started using a GLP-1 medication and lost 60 pounds.
That's how Jetty came to be.
Ellsworth's husband, Stephen, now CEO of the new brand, noticed she wasn't hydrating, even when she came back from the gym.
GLP-1 medications such as Ozempic and Mounjaro can make people less thirsty. But because staying hydrated can also help mitigate some of the drugs' side effects, such as nausea and headaches, it can become more important.
"I physically struggle getting liquid into my body," Ellsworth said.
Jetty is meant to solve that problem.
Plain old water is often less appealing to consumers, even dehydrated GLP-1 users, but more flavorful options with added benefits can be tempting. About 44% of GLP-1 users report consuming more functional beverages, according to EY-Parthenon's third annual survey of more than 3,600 current or former GLP-1 users.
Ellsworth sees a broader appeal for Jetty, too.
"Our core audience is going to be millennial moms and Gen Z," she said. "Gen Z just isn't relating to these old school brands, the legacy of the Gatorades and the Powerades. They're just not cool."
Consumers broadly have become more interested in staying hydrated.
Dollar sales of hydration and electrolyte products climbed 20% to $2.6 billion over the 52 weeks ended Oct. 4, based on data from SPINS, which tracks new universal product codes, or UPCs. The category also has a strong repeat buyer rate of 62%.
However, the Ellsworths aren't the only ones to notice the potential in hydration. The number of new items in the category with annual sales of at least $10,000 has increased 41% over the last two years, according to SPINS.
Big food and beverage companies have been looking to hydration, too.
Kraft Heinz debuted Capri Sun juice pouches and Kool-Aid packets with electrolytes this spring. In April, Pepsi unveiled an overhaul of the Gatorade brand, focused on making it more appealing to a wider swath of consumers, with more potential occasions like a "fresh morning start" or an "afternoon walk." And Electrolit is a top performer for its distributor Keurig Dr Pepper , with 40% retail sales growth in the company's third quarter.
All of that means more competition for shelf space and consumers' "share of throat," an industry term for beverage market share.
To increase Jetty's visibility across the grocery store and to maximize convenience for shoppers, Jetty will be available in both powders and bottles.
Single-use electrolyte mixes are growing at a much faster clip than the ready-to-drink category, Ellsworth said, thanks to Unilever 's Liquid I.V. and smaller upstarts like LMNT. On Amazon alone, powders are a $1 billion category, according to Ellsworth.
The ready-to-drink, or RTD, sports beverages are a much larger market, but the category's sales are shrinking as consumers reach for other hydration options instead. Unit sales of sports drinks have fallen 9.1% from 2022 to 2026, according to Numerator data. And Coca-Cola has written down the value of BodyArmor by more than $1.7 billion after buying control of the brand for $5.6 billion in late 2021.
That doesn't worry Jetty's founders.
"Me and my husband know how to do RTD," Ellsworth said.
Jetty will launch with five flavors, including watermelon, orange mango, fruit punch, black raspberry and white cherry. All of them contain 100 milligrams of sodium, 310 milligrams of potassium and 100 milligrams of magnesium in a 15.2-ounce bottle or 15-gram packet.
In addition to electrolytes, Jetty products also contain B vitamins, 3 grams of fiber and 6 grams of sugar. It doesn't use artificial sweeteners or dyes, its founders say.
For comparison, a 20-ounce bottle of traditional Gatorade Thirst Quencher has about 270 milligrams of sodium and 80 milligrams of potassium, plus 34 grams of sugar. The sports drink brand is also phasing out artificial colors and promoting lower-sugar versions.
"What's really interesting about this product and this opportunity is we now can capture all those lapsed drinkers — or that generation that didn't even ever drink it in the first place," Ellsworth said.
Poppi's new owner knows about Jetty and the market it is trying to capture, too.
"I don't think [Pepsi] gets it, but what they do get is that the movement is changing, and they think that just by taking dyes out or doing 90% less sugar, they're going to capture this audience," Ellsworth said. "But that is very big corporate thinking."
She added that she believes Pepsi has missed the mark on advertising to Gen Z consumers across its portfolio, such as in its campaigns for Sprite competitor Starry.
Perhaps as an extension of that, Poppi's performance has been underwhelming under PepsiCo's ownership.
The food and beverage giant now estimates the fair value of potential performance-based payments to Poppi's prior owners is $12 million, Pepsi said in a regulatory filing in October. At the time of the deal, Pepsi promised an additional payment of $300 million if Poppi hit certain targets by the third quarter of 2027. The Ellsworths declined to comment on the filing to CNBC.
This time around, with one successful brand under their belts, Jetty's founders say they have learned from past mistakes. Those lessons should help Jetty as it launches at a much larger scale than Poppi did.
Three different claims lawyers have signed off on Jetty's packaging, according to Ellsworth. Poppi paid $8.9 million to settle class-action litigation alleging false advertising over its "gut healthy" claims.
For now, Jetty is entirely self-funded with $2.5 million, although Ellsworth said that the brand will likely raise money in 2027. This time, though, she said investors will probably look less like traditional venture capitalists.
"I want to bring in investors that bring value," Ellsworth said. Instead of a venture capitalist who is willing to invest $15 million, Jetty would rather consider investors who can only write a check for $1 million but have access to celebrities. "So then you're getting access to talent on a cheaper level and people that are invested in the brand."

articles.title_orig: King leads solemn Remembrance service at Cenotaph
articles.title_zh: King leads solemn Remembrance service at Cenotaph
articles.content_orig:
King Charles III led the nation in a solemn two-minute silence on Remembrance Sunday in London to honour veterans who had died in conflict.
On a stone-grey autumn morning, he laid a wreath at the Cenotaph in Whitehall before a march-past by 10,000 armed forces veterans.
That included a shrinking number of World War Two veterans, with 12 taking part this year, including 103-year-old Annie Duplock, who described it as a "very emotional day".
Meanwhile, the number of former prime ministers reached a record high, with nine lined up to lay wreaths, while Andy Burnham attended for the first time as the current occupant of No 10 Downing Street.
And for the first time, the leader of Reform UK, Nigel Farage, had enough MPs in Parliament to qualify to lay a wreath alongside other major party leaders.
The Prince of Wales and the Princess Royal were among royals in attendance, along with military chiefs, senior politicians, diplomats and faith leaders, watched by big crowds squeezed behind railings along Whitehall.
Queen Camilla and the Princess of Wales watched from a balcony above the Cenotaph in the Foreign Office.
Among the flags on the roof of that Whitehall building was the Ukrainian blue and yellow. It went up when Russia invaded and four years later it is now visibly frayed - a reminder of the length of that war and of current threats.
At 11:00 GMT, as the first strike of Big Ben echoed from the nearby Houses of Parliament, the big two-minute silence filled the usually frenetic streets, before the playing of the Last Post.
The King had his eyes closed, the crowds in Whitehall stopped for their own thoughts, in a rare moment of calm in the capital.
The poignant parade past the Cenotaph included representatives of about 340 different military and civilian groups, from the Royal Naval Association and the Royal Marines Association to Transport for London and the Royal National Lifeboat Institute.
Alongside those marching were flotillas of disability scooters and families helping veterans in wheelchairs.
Those who took part in WW2 are now increasingly frail - and there were 12 participants in the march-past compared to 20 last year. The oldest participant this year was aged 105.
Taking part for the first time was 103-year-old Annie Duplock, who had been part of the Land Army that had helped to feed the country at war.
She had joined the Land Army in 1940 as a 16-year-old, having lied about her age, and worked on a farm in Leicestershire.
"I feel very honoured to be taking part in the parade and to represent the Land Girls. I'm very excited, although a little apprehensive as I don't quite know what to expect," she said.
"I think it will be a very emotional day, bringing back memories of all those who didn't return home. It will be lovely to be there and remember them."
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the annual event was a time to "reflect on the selflessness and courage it takes to commit your life to protecting others".
He earlier announced that he wanted to tackle the problem of homelessness among ex-service personnel to "ensure that any veteran sleeping rough is offered appropriate accommodation before Christmas".
Mark Atkinson, the director general of the Royal British Legion, said: "As we come together on Remembrance Sunday, we pay tribute to all those who have served and sacrificed, from generations past to those still serving today."
For more than a century, this national Remembrance event has been held around the Cenotaph.
The monument was built as a focal point for honouring those who had fought and died in World War One, including those who had no grave, and as a place to mourn for those families who might not be able to visit war cemeteries overseas.
The word "cenotaph" means "empty tomb" in Greek and it was designed by the architect Sir Edwin Lutyens in a simple, austere style, with no sense of triumphalism and with almost no decoration.
The monument had been originally built in 1919 as a temporary, plaster and wood structure. But it proved so popular with the public that it was replaced in 1920 with a permanent version, in the same design but in stone.
It was opened at 11:00 on 11 November 1920 by King George V. His great-grandson, Charles, was there again, on an overcast morning 106 years later, to continue paying respect.

articles.title_orig: House Republicans demand answers from Nvidia CEO over reported Chinese spy ties
articles.title_zh: House Republicans demand answers from Nvidia CEO over reported Chinese spy ties
articles.content_orig:
'The Big Money Show' panel discusses China's espionage threat targeting tech companies amid a report of a spy plot targeting Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and the nation's struggling economy.
House Republicans are demanding answers from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang about his reported relationship with a Chinese intelligence asset, escalating scrutiny of whether Beijing gained access to sensitive U.S. technology through the chip giant’s business ties.
The request follows a New York Times report that Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen and Megaspeed executive, had been gathering information for Beijing and developed a close relationship with Jensen Huang.
The Times reported that President Donald Trump was briefed on the intelligence findings about a year ago but chose not to act.
SUSPECTED CHINESE INTELLIGENCE ASSET GAINED ACCESS TO NVIDIA CEO JENSEN HUANG: REPORT
Jensen Huang, President and CEO of NVIDIA, delivers a speech to business leaders during the APEC CEO summit on Oct. 31, 2025 in Gyeongju, South Korea. (Ezra Acayan/Getty Images / Getty Images)
The letter, dated Wednesday and released Thursday , says recent reports raise national security concerns about China’s access to sensitive U.S. technology and information.
The lawmakers are seeking details about Jensen Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang and Nvidia’s security protocols against foreign espionage.
The letter was signed by House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla.; Select Committee on China Chairman John Moolenaar, R-Mich.; and House Intelligence Committee Chairman Rick Crawford, R-Ark. They invited Huang to an in-person joint briefing on Nov. 18, one day after Nvidia is scheduled to report its third-quarter earnings.
"China’s access to that sensitive U.S. tech is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress," the lawmakers wrote, adding that Congress must determine whether U.S. national security was put at risk.
HOW US CEOS QUIETLY TEAMED UP WITH TRUMP TO GAIN LEVERAGE OVER CHINA
China's President Xi Jinping (R) and US President Donald Trump visit the Temple of Heaven on May 14, 2026 in Beijing, China. (Brendan Smialowski - Pool/Getty Images / Getty Images)
It is unclear if Huang will attend. Nvidia did not immediately respond to FOX Business' request for comment.
The Times reported that U.S. officials initially did not believe Jensen Huang knew Alice Huang was allegedly gathering intelligence for China . It remains unclear whether that assessment has changed. Huang has not received a defensive briefing from the government, according to the Times.
The scrutiny comes as Jensen Huang has lobbied the Trump administration to loosen restrictions on Nvidia chip sales to China .
Earlier this year, Huang joined Trump’s business delegation to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping. He was reportedly added to the trip at the last minute and secured a seat on Air Force One, underscoring Nvidia’s role in U.S.-China trade and technology talks.
The delegation brought together executives from major U.S. companies with deep ties to China, including Apple CEO Tim Cook, Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Micron CEO Sanjay Mehrotra and Meta’s Dina Powell McCormick. Financial leaders Stephen Schwarzman of Blackstone, Larry Fink of BlackRock, Jane Fraser of Citigroup and David Solomon of Goldman Sachs also joined the trip.
CHINA ‘THROWING GASOLINE ON THE FIRE’ IN AI DATA CENTERS RACE, SAY LAWMAKERS
Graphic labels key CEOs in attendance at a high-profile meeting with President Donald Trump and Chinese officials. (Official White House Photo by Daniel Torok/Fox News)
Many of the executives are among the world’s wealthiest business leaders. Musk is the richest person in the world, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, while Schwarzman and Huang have fortunes in the tens of billions.
Together, their companies represent trillions of dollars in corporate power and rely on Chinese consumers, manufacturing and supply chains, even as Washington and Beijing clash over trade, technology and national security.
U.S. officials suspect some chips acquired by Megaspeed may have been smuggled into China.

articles.title_orig: Villa Vie Odyssey "forever cruise" residents want their ship back
articles.title_zh: Villa Vie Odyssey "forever cruise" residents want their ship back
articles.content_orig:
As the Villa Vie Odyssey cruise ship makes its way from Cambodia to Singapore, where it could potentially be auctioned off by its lender, CBS News has learned of at least two resident-led efforts to reclaim the vessel.
One effort recently failed after a lender denied funding to residents of the luxury "forever cruise." However, a second effort to buy the ship is still very much active, according to two sources familiar with the matter. It is led by another group hoping to buy the ship at auction, the sources said.
The second effort would not involve Villa Vie Residences' founder and executive chairman Mike Petterson, according to sources involved in the discussions.
Petterson said he believed he had an operational partner to rescue the ship, but that did not pan out, which led to the ship being taken by its lender.
Now, Petterson says he believes he could still get the ship back and is continuing to look for potential investors to take over the ship for good. Another option would be to raise the funds to file for Chapter 11 bankruptcy and sell the company. He no longer wants to be involved in company leadership.
"I'm not going to be the front face person of a company any time soon," Petterson told CBS News.
CBS News has also learned that a group of residents is considering legal action over fuel loans that were provided to the company in April — when residents said they raised more than $2 million dollars to keep the ship afloat.
The fuel loan program promised up to a 24% return if residents invested more money to help with the rising cost of fuel.
In a copy of an agreement obtained by CBS News, which appears to be from Villa Vie, the loan is described as "Unsecured" without "Collateral or Guarantees."
Craig and Cindy Voight were on board the ship from October 2024 when the Odyssey departed Belfast, Northern Ireland, for its voyage around the world . The couple said they spent more than $300,000 on their cabin and monthly dues, in addition to providing the company with $100,000 as participants in the fuel loan program. They said they plan to take legal action over that program.
"So we thought, alright, we're going to get 18% interest," Craig Voight said.  "First payment's supposed to start a month later. So between then and now they owe us over $113,000. They've never paid one penny."
Petterson acknowledged that some residents could potentially take legal action over the fuel loans in a statement that he shared with CBS News, saying "I take their concerns seriously."
In his statement, the executive also said financing for the loan program "was arranged during an urgent period for the vessel and was intended to support immediate operating needs, including fuel." The financing was structured through Villa Vie's parent company, Residential Cruise Holdings, "because existing financing restrictions prevented Villa Vie Residences from borrowing directly," he said.
"I recognize that residents want clear answers about how the loans were structured and handled," said Petterson. "Because legal action is being considered, I won't discuss individual claims or draw conclusions in the media. We will address the matter through the appropriate legal process and provide information through the proper channels."
This story published first on CBS News at 8:28 a.m. on Nov. 8, 2026.

articles.title_orig: Using miles to fly for Thanksgiving? These are the most expensive and cheapest routes
articles.title_zh: Using miles to fly for Thanksgiving? These are the most expensive and cheapest routes
articles.content_orig:
Airline ticket prices have surged this year, especially for travel over the holidays. Don't expect many bargains if you're booking flights with miles, either.
Tickets bought with frequent flyer miles for flights between large U.S. airports over the Thanksgiving travel period will cost 32% more than last year's holiday, according to data from Seats.aero, a miles and points redemption search site. While fares have skyrocketed this year, airline executives last month said demand remains strong.
Airlines have largely gotten rid of static mileage redemption charts in favor of dynamic pricing, making budgeting for an award ticket more difficult. Dynamic pricing means redemption costs change depending on demand, routes and other factors.
Many of the most expensive routes this Thanksgiving are understandably longer, including from Hawaii, but the list also includes a nonstop from New York to Houston.
Here's how mileage redemptions for the holiday are stacking up, based on one-way flights on average as of early November and compared with last year:
Jet fuel prices have surged since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28, which has eaten into airline profits. Carriers have sought to pass costs along to consumers as much as possible.
Even some of the cheapest routes for award tickets are more expensive than last year, including for short routes like Tulsa, Oklahoma, to Dallas Fort Worth International Airport.

articles.title_orig: Rumour: Pokemon Winds & Waves was delayed from November 2026 and caused big scheduling issues
articles.title_zh: Rumour: Pokemon Winds & Waves was delayed from November 2026 and caused big scheduling issues
articles.content_orig:
New nuggets of information have emerged regarding the long-awaited next mainline Pokemon game entry Pokemon Winds and Pokemon Waves for the Nintendo Switch 2 . The games were apparently scheduled for this month, but were pushed back at the last moment as they simply were not ready for release. This in turn caused massive scheduling issues for The Pokemon Company across its games and media.
I imagine it caused massive scheduling issues for Nintendo too as they would have needed to adjust all their other releases to account for the hole it left. You have to say it’s impressive that it hasn’t noticeably shown up like that.
This never happened before with them. It seems like all their plans has been sabotage. Doing stuff in the last minute is never a no go.
IMO worth it though. The games deserve that time to cook. Excited for what they have in store just gimme gen 3 and colosseum while I wait lol
Yeah I can agree the most.
A Pokemon game, being delayed? What’s next, pigs can fly?
I think a third legends game has been scrapped. I’m still ok with winds and waves needs a little more time to be in the oven but I get that people don’t want to wait any longer.
One extra year in the oven would not have saved ScarVi from its litteny of underlying issues, primarily the sheer incompetence of seemingly nearly every cook in the kitchen (not you creature design artists) and I don’t see how anyone thinks it could possibly save anything else made my the same team. Even if it runs at a rock solid 60fps with no bugs, the core design philosophy of the studio is just bafflingly amateur for such a high profit property. It NEEDS to be co-developed by a third party or a Nintendo in-house themselves for anyone but the hopelessly addicted/naive to get anything of real value from it. THat’s not to say it won’t sell well anyways, it obviously will no matter what, which is how we got here.
No edit button? Pardon the typos. Everyone will hate me anyways.

articles.title_orig: Cornwall artist who put camel in eye of needle plans exhibition
articles.title_zh: Cornwall artist who put camel in eye of needle plans exhibition
articles.content_orig:
Artist Adrian Thompson has created micro art from small pieces of gold that fit through the eye of a needle.
He said he enjoyed challenging himself to see what he could create.
Thompson, who works in Par, said: "As an artist sometimes it's you versus yourself. You want to see what you can create."
Each tiny piece takes up to a year to make and he is planning to display it at Bodmin's Discovering 42 science museum in December.
He started out transforming his gold dental filling, which had fallen out, into an angel when he lived in his home town of Solihull, near Birmingham.
Thompson used a file and said: "It slowly came to life over a period of about nine months, to my amazement."
He added: "Each times I picked it up I did a little bit more and a little bit more and got more inspiration. When I finally finished it I thought I really enjoyed it, I wonder what else I could be doing."
Thompson uses a microscope and had to customise watch maker's tools or make his own tiny tools to create his art.
He has placed his work in the eye of a needle, on the end of a needle and on a cat's whisker.
He also mounted a mini helicopter on an eyelash, which is one of the piece's people will be able to see in Bodmin.
Thompson created a microscope viewing dome for his pieces, which include a Ferrari horse on the end of a match stick valued at £100,000, the Aston Villa lion logo that was displayed at the club and a waving cat.
In the run-up to Halloween he made a microscopic gold witch flying out of an syringe point of a needle, along with a small Cornish pixie.
He said: "I've got many pieces to entertain people covering a range of different subjects.
"I've got quite a big car collection and what I call a 007 collection, which consists of Aston Martin wing DBS badge, and the 007 logo, all through the eye of a needle."
He added: "I've also created a standing Buddha out of white gold, a Chinese god called Caishen which fits on a meteorite, and a camel through the eye of a needle, so there is plenty of variety in my work."

articles.title_orig: Saudi Aramco Tower Damaged as Yemen’s Houthis Attack Riyadh
articles.title_zh: Saudi Aramco Tower Damaged as Yemen’s Houthis Attack Riyadh
articles.content_orig:
Iranian media suggested explosions in southern Iran on Saturday evening were related to Iranian military activities rather than U.S. strikes, while both sides reported that shipping had been hit in or near the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran's state television said officials had not confirmed any missile strikes on Iranian territory following blasts heard in several areas, including on Qeshm Island in the strait.
President Donald ​Trump had hinted at renewing major attacks on Iran ​after ⁠last week's US midterm elections but there has been no sign of a large-scale U.S. military operation, which Iran has said it would respond to by striking U.S. and Israeli targets.
Both sides have continued strikes on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, however, restricting exports of energy and other commodities vital to the world economy.
Iran's state television said the evening explosions might be related to Iranian military activity in the waterway, where Iran said two vessels had hit mines and a third had caught fire.
The US said its air force had disabled a vessel in the Gulf of Oman beyond the strait.
Tasnim news agency said two missiles had struck Qeshm Island, with no official information on possible damage. Neither Iran nor the US has commented on that report. Washington said on November 2 that it had struck the island in a limited defensive measure against Iranians using surface-to-air missiles against US assets.
Since the US and Israel began attacks on Iran in February, Tehran has sought the upper hand by hitting vessels in the Strait of Hormuz to block Gulf energy exports, while US forces began blockading movements to and from Iranian ports in April.
The U.S. military said on Saturday evening that its air force had fired at the stern of a commercial vessel in the Gulf of Oman, disabling it as it tried to get through the blockade.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy said two oil tankers had caught fire after hitting mines while attempting to pass through an "unauthorized route" in the Strait of Hormuz. A third tanker had also suffered an explosion and caught fire, the semi-official Fars news agency reported later.
Reuters could not confirm any of the reported strikes.
Monitors from the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said a bulk carrier and military forces were involved in an incident in the Gulf of Oman, approximately 18 nautical miles east of the United Arab Emirates' city of Khor ⁠Fakkan, with damage unknown. It was unclear if it was related to the reported US attack.
A conflict between Iran-aligned Houthis in Yemen and Saudi Arabia has escalated this month, enlarging the wider Middle East war.
On Sunday, Saudi Arabia's energy ministry said an administrative building belonging to state oil company Saudi Aramco in Riyadh had been damaged by falling debris after an attempted attack, with no injuries or fatalities reported.
Qatar, which has been mediating talks to end the conflict that has shaken the world economy, on Saturday denied reports that the U.S. and Iran had failed to reach a deal.
The Qatari prime minister had ​affirmed that both sides were continuing ​to ⁠work toward an agreement, it said.
Iran has submitted a nuclear proposal to Washington through Qatar, a senior Iranian official told Reuters on Thursday, saying the U.S. was reviewing it, but discussions would depend on Washington first meeting Tehran's seven demands.
These include sanctions relief, access to frozen assets and war reparations, while Washington insists nuclear issues must be part of initial talks.
On Saturday, the US military said it was launching a task force to crack down on the movement of advanced weapons and other sanctioned material to Iran via its land borders and the Caspian Sea – part of economic measures to try to pressure Tehran.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards dismissed the plan as "wordplay," saying it would not work because Tehran had prepared and coordinated closely with its neighbors.

articles.content_orig:
Russia played a larger role in the Iran war than previously disclosed, with internal defense industry documents revealing how Moscow built up the country's arsenal ahead of its conflict with the U.S.
A Russian contract is tied to 90 launchers for precision-guided missiles with the destination as Tehran, according to documents obtained and published by Ukrainian defense intelligence research group Dallas Analytics offering new details on the extent of Moscow's military support for Iran before war erupted.
President Donald Trump has repeatedly downplayed Russia's role in the conflict — as recently as last month, saying that he did not believe they are helping Iran "at all."
Russian production records show components were allocated for 90 APU-L twin-rail launchers under a contract identified as "K-10," with shipments within the Russian production chain scheduled from late 2024 through December 2025.
Other internal Russian documents obtained by Dallas Analytics explicitly identify "K-10" as Iran. An October 2022 supply request for equipment for a Yak-130 aircraft lists the consignee as "'K10' Iran" and was countersigned by the acting head of the Russian Defense Ministry's 704th Military Representation.
The K-10 designation can also be traced to Russian military hardware that ultimately reached Iran. An internal Russian production schedule listed six Yak-130 aircraft for a consignee identified as K-10. Iranian state media later showed the aircraft entering service in September 2023, and Dallas Analytics said the tail number of one Iranian Yak-130 matched the number listed for K-10 in the Russian factory records.
This is an excerpt from an article by Fox News' Morgan Phillips.
This is an excerpt from an opinion article by Robert Maginnis, a retired U.S. Army infantry officer, senior fellow for National Security at the Family Research Council.
Twenty years ago, American voters punished Republicans over an unpopular war in the Middle East. On Nov. 3, they did it again.
In 2006, it was Iraq. This time, it was Iran. Democrats captured both houses of Congress, flipping at least seven Senate seats, including Texas, Ohio, Kansas and Iowa. Vice President JD Vance put the blame squarely where President Donald Trump would rather not have it: on the war his administration launched eight months ago.
I remember the earlier debacle. As a Pentagon strategist during the run-up to the 2003 Iraq invasion, I attended meetings with Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld and senior military leaders. I questioned whether the administration had adequately considered what would follow Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein’s overthrow.
Now Trump faces a reckoning of his own. American forces have inflicted tremendous damage on Iran’s military. But military success does not guarantee strategic success, especially when the American people lose confidence in the mission.
Vance was blunt in his Nov. 4 assessment: "The reason we lost is the war." He dared anyone to argue that "losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it."
Trump acknowledged that the war contributed to Republican losses but defended his decision: "I would have done nothing differently." He added, "You can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon."
He is right about that. But the election raises a question his administration has yet to answer: What has eight months of fighting accomplished that will last?
I have consistently argued that a nuclear-armed Iran is unacceptable. In June 2025, I supported decisive action against Tehran’s deeply buried Fordow nuclear facility. Four days later, however, I challenged claims that Iran was only weeks away from producing a usable nuclear weapon. The intelligence did not publicly establish that conclusion.
Israeli President Isaac Herzog announced Saturday that he has chosen opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot to form the country's next government, handing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's chief rival the first opportunity to build a coalition following an inconclusive national election.
Herzog announced his decision on Nov. 7, but the formal presentation of the mandate is scheduled for Sunday, Nov. 8, at 5 p.m. Israeli time. Eisenkot will then have 28 days to assemble a government, with a possible 14-day extension.
The decision could mark a significant step toward ending Netanyahu’s tenure, but it would also launch a difficult round of coalition negotiations, with deep disagreements among parties seeking to replace him.
Following two days of consultations with Israel’s newly elected parliament, Herzog announced Thursday that factions representing 67 of the Knesset’s 120 members had recommended Eisenkot, chairman of the Yashar party, to form the next government. Netanyahu received the backing of 46 lawmakers, while seven members of the ultra-Orthodox United Torah Judaism party declined to endorse either candidate.
"The results of the consultations may appear clear," Herzog said in his Nov. 5 statement, but cautioned that competing political demands and vetoes have left the prospects for forming a government uncertain.
The challenge facing Eisenkot is that the 67 endorsements do not translate into a 67-seat governing coalition.In the Oct. 27 election, Netanyahu’s Likud emerged as the largest single party with 27 seats, while his wider political bloc won 53. The four-party alliance seeking to replace him secured just 48 seats.
This is an excerpt from an article by Fox News Efrat Lachter.
Secretary of War Pete Hegseth is facing a bipartisan impeachment threat when Congress returns next week as Republicans seethe over their devastating losses in Tuesday's midterm elections.
Bipartisan frustration over the war in Iran, quietly simmering for months, is now openly erupting after Democrats stunned the country with historic victories in the House and Senate. That anger could all now hit Hegseth, with several House Republicans telling Fox News Digital that they believe a resolution to impeach him could pass as early as next week.
"He's screwed," one House GOP lawmaker told Fox News Digital.
Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., a longtime critic of foreign intervention by the U.S., told Fox News Digital he intends to force a vote on impeaching Hegseth when Congress returns if the Pentagon chief does not resign first.
He'll do so by filing a privileged resolution, a mechanism aimed at getting a vote on legislation despite opposition from the majority party's leaders. Once a privileged resolution is filed, lawmakers have two legislative days to hold a vote.
But the procedure notably carries two steps. Before a vote on the measure itself, leaders can call up a vote to "table" the bill or refer it to the relevant committee, which in both instances effectively kills it.
That procedural vote is normally where most privileged resolutions die. But in this case, several House Republicans told Fox News Digital they believe the impeachment resolution could ultimately be successful.

Hoffman remains skeptical that the U.S. and Iran will come to a negotiated settlement in the near future.
Trump has not ruled out a return to full scale war.

We already know of one surprise, which is that eight games will be joining Xbox Game Pass Essential on the 15th itself. Combine that with the six others during the rest of the week, and we've got over 10 brand-new additions heading to Game Pass during the course of the 25th anniversary period.
In case you missed them, those eight Game Pass Essential games on the 15th are as follows:
As for the rest, we've got three games arriving on the 10th, two arriving on the 11th, and one on the 12th. There's every chance Microsoft might add to these as we go, but these are the ones that have been confirmed so far.
A highlight for many will be John Carpenter's Toxic Commando on November 12th, which is an awesome take on the classic Left 4 Dead formula, while all the others are "day one" launches, including the extremely addictive Football Manager 27 , the Vampire Survivors-like Warhammer Survivors , and BMX postman game Tanuki: Pon's Summer .
Instead of just throwing these ones into a table, we're going to leave them down below with trailers and descriptions, and we'll be sure to remind you on the relevant dates when they become available with your Game Pass subscription.
Choose the club. Shape the squad. Set the tactics. Chase the future only you can see. FM27 is where your footballing beliefs become a reality. Make The Call.
The Tanuki Festival is just a month away, and the shrine is in disrepair. Follow Pon, a well meaning, if a bit lazy Tanuki with a part-time job at the Post Office, as he works to restore the shrine before summer ends. Deliver packages, make friends, and get the shrine ready for the big festival!
Warhammer Survivors is the official grim and dark bullet-heaven game from the developers of Warhammer 40,000 Boltgun. Play as over 40 iconic champions from the Warhammer 40,000 and Warhammer Age of Sigmar universes and obliterate those who champion death and destruction.
17-year-old Hope Song thought the national exams were her biggest worry... until she got home to a ransacked apartment and two missing parents. Investigate through the eyes of an artist, turn sketches into evidence, and watch her family's mystery grow stranger and darker with every answer.
Thronefall is a minimalist strategy game where you build a humble kingdom by day and defend it by night. Balance economy and defense by fortifying walls, recruiting troops, and charging into battle yourself to protect your stronghold from relentless waves of attackers.
Pick a character and team up with three friends ‘cause it’s time to save the world. Experience intense FPS action as you obliterate hordes of terrifying monsters! You may not be on the best team of mercenaries, but you are… a Toxic Commando!

articles.title_orig: CEO SUNDAY: Army veteran turned health tech boss calls support for those who served a 'sacred obligation'
articles.title_zh: CEO SUNDAY: Army veteran turned health tech boss calls support for those who served a 'sacred obligation'
articles.content_orig:
Philips North America CEO Jeff DiLullo shares how his Army service shaped his leadership, career and commitment to supporting veterans.
Long after Jeff DiLullo traded his Army uniform for a suit, a lesson from his years at West Point and in the military has stayed with him: the importance of serving "something bigger" than himself.
As CEO of Philips North America, a global health technology company that makes medical equipment used in hospitals, DiLullo has found a new way to put that lesson into practice through his work supporting veterans and their families.
"One of the most rewarding things for me personally that I've brought from my military service into my corporate life is a sense of service and serving something bigger than myself," DiLullo told FOX Business. "And now today, I do that through serving our veteran community."
BUILT FROM SCRATCH: HOW A RENTED KITCHEN AND HAND-SQUEEZED FRUIT BECAME A VERSATILE MIXER
He added, "To me, it's a sacred obligation as a nation to serve our veterans and not only them, but their families and caregivers too."
DiLullo graduated from the United States Military Academy at West Point with a bachelor's degree in history before serving as an infantry officer in the U.S. Army. He later earned an MBA in marketing , logistics and supply chain from the University of Tennessee's Haslam College of Business.
GOOGLE PARTNERS WITH VETERANS GROUPS TO HELP 25,000 ENTER SKILLED TRADES CAREERS AMID WORKER SHORTAGE
As CEO of Philips North America, DiLullo has found a new way to put that lesson into practice through his work supporting veterans and their families. (Philips North America)
His connection to military service has only become more personal in recent years. DiLullo's daughter and son-in-law are both currently on active duty, and he knows firsthand that eventually leaving the military can bring its own challenges.
"When you leave the military, you wonder if you're going to maintain the connection to a mission and something important and purposeful," DiLullo said. "Many veterans struggle with that transition just like I did."
After leaving the Army, he built a successful career in corporate America, eventually holding executive leadership positions at Hewlett-Packard, Avaya and Dell.
"After the Army, honestly, I buried myself in work," he said. "I tried to find a sense of purpose and mission in what I was doing, and I had great jobs, but I hit a wall, and I was trying to do everything well but not feeling that I was really deeply connected to my own sense of purpose."
The realization ultimately pushed him to rethink what he wanted from his career.
"After a period of reflection, almost 10 years ago, I decided to just change course completely," he said. "I moved into healthcare and I decided I would only work where I felt a personal sense of purpose, and I have never looked back. I'm having the most fun I've had in my entire career."
VETERAN-OWNED TEA COMPANY AIMS TO HELP FORMER SERVICE MEMBERS ‘FIND PURPOSE’
DiLullo joined Philips in 2019 as head of North America operations.
That path eventually brought DiLullo to Philips, where he joined the company in 2019 as head of North America operations. His responsibilities expanded in 2021 to include leadership of the company's North America services and solutions delivery teams.
Today, DiLullo said his work has given him a renewed connection to the sense of mission he valued in the military.
The Department of Veterans Affairs is Philips' largest customer , according to DiLullo, and he also serves on the board of the Elizabeth Dole Foundation, which supports military and veteran caregivers.
"These things are fuel for me and really fuel my sense of purpose and connection and service," he said.
Asked what advice he would offer today's West Point cadets, DiLullo said their commitment to the country does not have to end when their military careers do.
"You've taken a solemn vow to serve and defend your nation ," he said. "You have willingly taken up the responsibility to protect the freedoms that are the foundation of this great country."
DiLullo added, "Service does not end when you leave the military. Your oath is to a lifetime of service to the nation. So my advice will be always to know and serve something bigger than yourself."
VETERANS ARE USING THIS HOMEBUYING BENEFIT MORE OFTEN — BUT MANY STILL DON’T KNOW IT EXISTS
DiLullo graduated from the United States Military Academy at West Point with a bachelor's degree in history before serving as an infantry officer in the U.S. Army. (Rich Graessle/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)
Among all the roles DiLullo has held since leaving the military, one still stands apart.
CLICK HERE TO GET FOX BUSINESS ON THE GO
"I can honestly say, other than the military, this is the most fulfilling work I've ever done," he said of his work in healthcare.
But the best job he ever had?
"The best job I ever had was the Army," DiLullo said. "A sense of mission, teamwork, and trust. It just defined my ideal world."

articles.title_orig: I lost my tech job and couldn't afford my mortgage. Now I live in a 100-square-foot shed in the yard.
articles.title_zh: I lost my tech job and couldn't afford my mortgage. Now I live in a 100-square-foot shed in the yard.
articles.content_orig:
This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Lauren Patton, 36, who built a tiny home in her Texas backyard. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity.
After a couple of years of living in Chicago, I decided to move back to Texas and get a fresh start. This was in 2022, when the real estate market was booming, and homes in Central Texas were getting bought up quickly.
I found a real estate agent on Instagram, and she helped me buy a small bungalow — two bedrooms and about 1,000 square feet — for about $400,000. I was buying alone; it was just me and my dog.
I had made a very small down payment on my home and taken out a 30-year mortgage. My monthly payment was about $4,000, which was a lot at first, but I thought it was affordable given my well-paying job.
At the time, I was working in tech and doing really well. I had been moving up the data science ladder, and I thought it would be a lucrative field. But I was a bit wrong about that.
In early 2023, there were a bunch of tech layoffs . I found out the day after I got back from a trip to South Africa that I had been let go. I was given only two months of severance and sent on my way.
For the first couple of months after I was laid off , I was OK. I took time to relax, spent time with my family, and did the things you don't get to do while you're working. Then I started looking for jobs.
I wasn't super worried at first. I thought, "Hey, I was a data science manager. I'll be able to find something." But after interviewing at numerous places, nothing was happening.
By then, money was tight. I had very little savings and was still paying off a lot of credit card debt. I filed for unemployment, which brought in some money, and started renting out my home on Airbnb to help cover my mortgage.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
To make this work, I rented a room for myself across town for about six months. But when my unemployment ran out, I had to start crashing on people's couches and driving for Lyft— basically doing whatever I could.
In 2024, I reached out to a former boss and asked if I could get my previous accounting job back. I did, and while it paid much less than I was making before, it sustained me for a while.
Still, I had no savings, and I had cashed out my 401(k) . I was terrified. My mortgage was just so much; I thought my home was going to go into foreclosure. I was already about 30% underwater on the home, and it had depreciated in value, so I still didn't want to sell.
I was 35 and thought, "I can't keep doing this." I knew I needed to do something. That's when I came up with the idea to build a little structure in my backyard to live in.
I wasn't confident enough in my woodworking or carpentry skills, so I decided to buy a cabin-style shed kit I found out about on Instagram. I took out a loan and bought it for about $8,500.
While I was building the shed , I moved back into my main house and got a roommate to help cover the mortgage. I charged about $1,200 a month for the room. It wasn't a huge portion of my mortgage payment, but it helped. Looking back, I regret buying a two-bedroom house, because there just aren't enough bedrooms to rent out.
The shed is about 100 square feet, and the kit came with stackable wood slats, beams, and big windows, but it didn't include a roof or a floor. I had to build the foundation , too. I also added an outhouse with an outdoor shower and built fences and other things around the property.
For the construction, I relied on YouTube and ChatGPT — though ChatGPT definitely led me astray on a few things, especially the roofing.
I officially finished the build in March 2025, though I've been making adjustments ever since — it's never-ending.
Since moving into the shed, I've been renting out my main home full-time on Airbnb and have hosted hundreds of guests.
I let Airbnb handle the pricing. On a typical weekend night, I charge around $200; on a weekday during the school year, it's closer to $125.
October is especially lucrative because of the Austin City Limits music festival. This October, my home had about 96% occupancy, and my gross earnings were about $6,516.70. That's not normal — occupancy and nightly rates were higher — but Airbnb deducted $619 in service fees. I also had the home cleaned seven times for about $100 each time.
I put some of the money I earned toward my mortgage and bills for the shed — my total electric bill, including the shed and the house, is $550, which also includes other utilities.
But overall, Airbnb doesn't cover my full mortgage, which increased by $400 a month this year because of home insurance.
It was tough at first, downsizing to a tiny home . Emotionally, it felt like I was regressing in life, and physically, it felt really claustrophobic. But I don't mind it as much now. I'm doing better mentally.
I have most of what I need in a normal house — a TV, a desk, and a bed. But I have a tiny, itty-bitty fridge, and I don't have ice or running water, so I have to stock up on jugs of water.
I've had to learn a lot about how to live in the space . When I first moved in, I had a portable air conditioner, and the humidity would reach 80%. I'd wake up soaking wet and think, "What's going on?" I'd never had to consider something like that before. Now, I run a dehumidifier 24 hours a day.
The hardest part is remembering to keep everything I need on hand, because there's always one thing missing. I'll go to grill chicken and realize I'm out of salt, or that it's back in the main house. I'm constantly running out to buy little things, and sometimes I wonder whether it's really financially worth it.
Some days, I think, "Man, this is harder than I thought it was going to be."
At this point, I've tried literally everything I can do to keep my home — I mean everything. If things don't get better in the next couple of years, I'll be comfortable letting it go, because I know I tried my hardest.
Looking back, I wish I had done more research as a first-time homebuyer . Aside from a high mortgage, my house is also like 100 years old, so it often needs repairs. I thought I was handy and could do it all myself, but it really wears on your soul.
I also wish I had thought more about the financial worst-case scenario. You hear advice from your parents: Don't let your mortgage take up too much of your income. I wish I had listened and hadn't gone over that 30% threshold .
The next time I buy a home, I need to stay under it. I also can't be so optimistic. I need to be more realistic, because this has shifted my life so much.
A couple of weeks ago, I started posting about my layoff and the shed on social media. It's really taken off; I've gained around 12,000 followers on Instagram .
I'm really grateful. Most people have been so great and lovely. And while I haven't earned any money from my reels yet, I'm working on it.
As for a job, I'm currently working on a data analytics project and am still walking dogs. My income from my jobs doesn't cover my mortgage, but I'm just grateful to have a job at all.
I feel sorry for people getting laid off, and I can definitely relate. When I'm back on my feet and in a better place financially, I want to help as many people in similar situations as I can.
One day, I'd like to move back into the main house and rent out the shed for a few hundred dollars to someone who needs an affordable place to live.
