articles.title_orig: Asia Power Snapshot: China, the United States, and the race for AI dominance
articles.title_zh: Asia Power Snapshot: China, the United States, and the race for AI dominance
articles.content_orig:
Subscribe to The Informer for monthly expert analysis, and to Events for advance notice of visiting world leaders and distinguished guests.
You may unsubscribe from Lowy Institute newsletters at any time. For information on our privacy practices and how to unsubscribe, see our Privacy Policy .
Who is winning the AI race between the United States and China? The answer depends on what you measure.
Photo: Jason Edwards/Getty
Asia Power Snapshot: China, the United States, and the race for AI dominance
US President Donald Trump has declared that “whoever wins AI wins,” suggesting that the competition for mastery over artificial intelligence (AI) is the pre-eminent geopolitical contest of the day. But who is winning the AI race between the United States and China? The answer depends on what you measure. This Data Snapshot compares the inputs and outputs that matter most — from chips and compute to research and innovation — to show which side holds the lead, where the gaps are narrowing, and where capabilities may be overstated.
Based on a thorough analysis of available data, including 14 indicators across four measures — Resources, Technology, AI capabilities, and AI adoption — the United States is currently leading the race. However, its lead is far from uniform, and the competition remains uneven across multiple domains. The United States is well ahead in AI capabilities, driven by its dominance in compute, and in AI adoption, where its lead in web traffic and apps outweighs China’s edge in open models. By contrast, China has a clear lead in Resources, particularly critical minerals — the key materials needed for manufacturing the advanced technologies that make AI possible. Governance, however, remains contested. Neither superpower is widely trusted to regulate AI, leaving room for middle powers such as Australia to help shape the rules.
China holds a clear advantage over the United States in both production and known reserves of critical minerals.
In November 2025, the US Department of the Interior released a list of 60 minerals critical to its economic and national security interests. 1 China leads in production of 30, while the United States is ahead in only eight — with 22 not produced in either country. China holds larger known reserves of 20 listed minerals, and the United States of seven, with one tied, and insufficient data for the remaining 32.
China’s ability to impose targeted export controls on critical minerals poses a major risk for the United States. In 2023, Beijing began announcing restrictions on several, including gallium and germanium — both used in semiconductors. 2
To counter this vulnerability, the United States has sought to cooperate with other countries to secure critical minerals. It has developed Pax Silica, a 24-member international framework focused on AI-related supply chain resilience. 3 In Asia, it has critical minerals frameworks with Australia and Japan and has also signed memoranda of understanding with Malaysia and Thailand. 4 In February 2026, it held a Critical Minerals Ministerial meeting, where it signed an additional 11 bilateral agreements, including one with the Philippines. 5
* For more on the semiconductor supply chain in Asia, and Southeast Asia’s role as a connector between the United States and China, see Between the superpowers: Southeast Asia’s strategic supply chain dilemma (Opens in new window) .
The United States leads China in technological sophistication. While China has almost 11 million full-time equivalent researchers — over seven million more than the United States — US spending on research and development (R&D) is considerably higher as a share of GDP (3.45 per cent versus China’s 2.58 per cent). The United States also has a sizeable lead in the number of data centres and supercomputers.
The United States has sought to limit China’s access to advanced technologies that could help develop its semiconductor industry. Washington has imposed numerous restrictions on both China and Chinese subsidiaries abroad, which has, in turn, spurred affected companies to innovate around them. 6 In May 2026, Huawei announced a new chip-design approach intended to increase transistor density without shrinking transistors. This could allow it to design chips by 2031 with transistor density equivalent to that of the chips Taiwan’s TSMC aims to make in 2028, without the advanced lithography machines China is barred from importing. 7 If successful, this could limit the effect of US export controls.
While companies have looked for ways to work around US controls, Beijing has moved to expand its own, building on its critical mineral restrictions. In October 2026, China proposed adding 40 technologies to its restricted exports, including 23 related to AI — among them AI chip design, the core technology of the most advanced models, and AI tools, such as deepfake detection systems. 8
The United States maintains a lead in AI capabilities. Its AI data centres have nearly 40 times the combined computing power of China’s, and its AI chips 31 times. This has helped US models stay ahead in benchmark tests, though the margin is narrowing.
As of November 2026, the top US large language model (LLM) on Arena, a platform that ranks models through blind head-to-head comparisons, is Google’s Gemini 4 Carbon, with an estimated score of 1528, closely followed by Google’s Gemini 4 Argon at 1520 and Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 at 1509. China’s top model, Moonshot’s Kimi K3, released in mid-July 2026, scores an estimated 1488, placing it 19th. The last top US model at this level was Google’s Gemini 3 Pro, which led from its release in mid-November 2025 until late January 2026. This gap is consistent with claims that the United States has a six-to-nine-month lead in AI capabilities. 9
The global spread of LLMs is arguably the most important front in the AI race. The models that consumers, businesses, and governments rely on will shape the information they see, how their economies run, and, potentially, the future of war. Which country leads depends on how users access the models.
There are six main ways to do so:
Reliable data exist for four of these: websites, apps, self-hosted open models, and aggregator platforms.
China holds a comfortable lead in self-hosted open models and aggregator platforms. 10 In the third quarter of 2026, Chinese models were downloaded nearly 1.8 billion times on Hugging Face, compared with 500 million for US models, giving China 78 per cent of the two countries’ combined downloads. Such models particularly appeal to governments and businesses, which can run them on their own servers to keep data local and adapt them to their needs. On aggregator platform OpenRouter, Chinese models accounted for 55 per cent of all text requests in the week commencing 26 October 2026 — compared to the US share of 38 per cent.
However, most users access LLMs through websites, apps, and embedded AI. The United States has a commanding lead in websites and apps. US models drew more than 90 per cent of combined global traffic to US and Chinese AI websites. US models also accounted for more than 80 per cent of combined use of US and Chinese AI apps, based on Google Play downloads and, for China, where Google Play is unavailable, QuestMobile data.
Overall, most people who use AI rely on US models, giving the United States unmatched reach and greater influence over the technology’s global direction.
With no other country posing a challenge to their dominance in AI, the United States and China have an outsized influence over how the technology is governed globally.
Rival blocs are already taking shape. Washington launched Pax Silica in December 2025 to secure AI supply chains among trusted partners. Beijing answered in July 2026 with the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO), which centres on AI governance standards and digital development. Twenty-nine countries signed its founding agreement, and eight more have

articles.title_orig: Vinted and eBay could be included in under-16 social media ban, minister says
articles.title_zh: Vinted and eBay could be included in under-16 social media ban, minister says
articles.content_orig:
Vinted and eBay could be included in the list of platforms set to be banned for children aged under 16, the culture secretary has said.
Lisa Nandy said the government was "looking seriously" at including the retailing websites in the social media ban "to keep children safe".
The UK's social media ban for under-16s is set to come into force in March next year, with children barred from accessing platforms such as Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat.
In response, eBay said it was looking forward to "understanding more and continuing to work constructively with the government". Vinted said it welcomed "open dialogue" with ministers and the regulator on the issue.
Asked on the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme whether the government was looking to ban under-16s from Vinted and eBay, Nandy said: "We are looking seriously at doing so in order to keep children safe."
It came after the Sunday Times reported that the UK's social media ban was being expanded to include the popular second-hand online marketplaces.
The move was due to fears that messaging functions on the platforms allowed strangers to groom children, according to the newspaper. It suggested similar reselling platforms, Depop and Facebook Marketplace, would also be included in the list of banned sites.
Businesses and individuals sell a host of goods on eBay, which has been a major global player in the online reselling market for years. The platform states on its website that it currently requires all of its members to be over 18 years old because listings involve "entering into a contract".
Vinted is aimed at over 18s, but its terms and conditions do allow parents or guardians to create accounts for their children, which must be used under parental supervision.
The site, on which users mostly buy and sell unwanted clothes and other fashion items, has grown rapidly recently to reach 17 million UK users.
A Vinted spokesperson said direct messaging was "part of how the platform works" but that it had a "zero tolerance for harmful or explicit content" and had moderation teams and tools to spot and remove "activity that breaks our rules".
"When we identify inappropriate behaviour, we take action, up to a permanent ban or reporting to the relevant authorities," they said.
An eBay spokesperson said the company was "focused on providing a trusted and safe marketplace experience for our millions of customers".
"While the details of the proposed legislation are not yet clear, we look forward to understanding more and continuing to work constructively with the government," they added.
The government announced it would ban under-16s accessing social media in June this year, with children prevented from accessing 10 of the biggest platforms.
YouTube will also be banned for under-16s, but YouTube Kids - a version of the video-sharing app designed to be safe for children - will not be included in the measures.
A complete list of affected platforms has not yet been released, but the government said it would cover those "whose purpose is to enable social interaction and which allow users to post material".
That means platforms that have livestreaming or features that enable the potential for strangers to contact children will also be restricted, which includes gaming sites.
It does not mean that Roblox, the biggest gaming site in the UK for those aged eight to 12, for example, will be banned for under-16s. However, certain features such as its chat function will be restricted.
But Matthew Sinclair, a senior director at the Computer and Communications Industry Association, which represents tech companies, argued that ministers should prevent the rules having "scope creep".
He said a restriction on messaging for under-16s "would not stop at social media and would reach into the services families depend on to stay in touch", and urged the government to "ensure any new restrictions are proportionate and effective."
The UK's ban comes after a similar one was introduced in Australia last year.
Many children there have found ways to get round it, but the UK has said it intends to take a tougher approach.
In recent weeks, attention has turned to how a social media ban would be enforced.
Last month, the communications regulator Ofcom set out its recommendations for the most effective ways to identify which of the UK's millions of social media users are aged over 16.
Rani Govender, head of online child safety at the NSPCC, said the "real question" going forward was how the government ensured age checks were effective.
"But effective age checks are only part of the solution," she added. "Tech companies must also be required to build child safety into every platform, device and AI tool, so children are protected from harmful and illegal content and only able to access age-appropriate services."

articles.title_orig: Hundreds of thousands left without power in Ukraine after Russian strikes, authorities say
articles.title_zh: Hundreds of thousands left without power in Ukraine after Russian strikes, authorities say
articles.content_orig:
Hundreds of thousands of people were left without power after Russian strikes hit Ukraine's energy infrastructure, authorities said on Sunday.
In the central Dnipropetrovsk region, "more than 600,000 residents of the region have been left without power," power company DTEK said on Telegram after a "night attack has damaged important energy facilities".
It said the company was working to restore electricity but the task was "complicated by repeated attacks".
Ukrainian President Volodymyr previously accused Russia of ramping up attacks on Ukraine ahead of trilateral talks next week with Russia.
In another strike, a Russian drone hit "a critical infrastructure facility" in the northeastern Kharkiv region, the mayor of Zlatopil city, Mykola Baksheyev, said on social media.
"Nearly 250,000 customers in the Kharkiv region were left without power," Baksheyev said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the night-time strikes had triggered "widespread power outages across the country".
"In the Zhytomyr region alone, 140 apartment buildings were left without heating following a Russian strike," he said, as temperatures in Ukraine already hovered around freezing.
He also said Russia had launched a drone at Komyshuvakha, a village in the Zaporizhzhia region where Moscow had hit an aid distribution centre on Monday in one of the deadliest attacks of the war.
The death toll has risen to 55 people, Zelenskyy said. Emergency services previously put it at 50 killed.
"This morning, the Russians attacked Komyshuvakha with an FPV drone, where emergency rescue operations have been underway for seven days ... Unfortunately, more people may still be under the rubble," Zelenskyy said.
The strikes came a day after Ukraine's energy ministry said a massive attack on energy facilities had plunged residents in five regions into darkness and significantly hampered electricity transmission in Kyiv.

articles.title_orig: Have humpback whales been witnessed trying to send messages to humans? What could they be trying to tell us?
articles.title_zh: Have humpback whales been witnessed trying to send messages to humans? What could they be trying to tell us?
articles.content_orig:
Could humpback whales be trying to communicate with us?
Humpback whales have long been admired for their intelligence, and their behaviour around other marine creatures has been extensively observed and documented.
In particular, the whales’ habit of teaming up to blow bubbles and form a ring around a school of small fish to ‘corral’ them and make feeding easier. This hunting collaboration has raised interesting speculation about the nature of communication between team members.
In 2021, a team of scientists from the SETI Institute conducted what was termed a ‘conversation’ with a single humpback named Twain. This consisted of playing whale calls through an underwater speaker that Twain responded to with similar calls.
Later, in a 2024 study by the same group, whale calls made during bubble feeding events, originally thought to be random and purposeless apart, perhaps, from being a way to keep in touch with other members of the pod, were surmised to have more specific objectives. Certain calls seemed to be a way of the whales issuing instructions or making targeted comments to the group.
But these studies did not touch on humpback whales’ voluntary interactions with humans, rather than contact engineered by the researchers, or their use of bubble blowing, other than as a hunting strategy.
A 2025 study by the scientists from SETI and the University of California, published in Marine Mammal Science , addressed both these aspects of whale behaviour and documented humpbacks producing large bubble rings during friendly encounters with humans that seem to be an attempt at sending messages.
The SETI Institute’s overall purpose is to understand the origins and prevalence of life and intelligence in the universe so these interactions aroused great interest. Non-verbal communications, as well as attempts at speech, wherever they occur, are seen as key to furthering our understanding of all life forms. This applies to non-human species currently on Earth as well as to any sentient beings that might be encountered in the future, if space exploration brings us in communication contact with life forms on other planets.
“Humpback whales live in complex societies, are acoustically diverse, use bubble tools and assist other species being harassed by predators,” says co-lead author Dr Fred Sharpe. “Now, akin to a candidate signal, we show they are blowing bubble rings in our direction in an apparent attempt to playfully interact, observe our response, and/or engage in some form of communication.”
A candidate signal is the name given to interesting radio waves that can be detected from the depths of space, that have been the subject of much analysis as to their origin and meaning. The team likened what they see as these attempts at communication on the part of the whales, and the efforts researchers are making to understand their bubble messages, as akin to the work being done to interpret interplanetary radio signals.
The study analysed 12 bubble ring-production episodes involving 39 rings made by 11 individual whales. “We’ve now located a dozen whales from populations around the world, the majority of which have voluntarily approached boats and swimmers blowing bubble rings during these episodes of curious behaviour,” said co-lead author Jodi Frediani, a marine wildlife photographer.
The Whale-SETI team aims to use the results of their research to develop filters that aid in parsing cosmic signals for signs of extra-terrestrial life.
They hope that with continued observation and the help of AI they may in the future be able to accurately interpret the communications, verbal and non-verbal, of whales and other animals. These learnings and techniques could then be applied to communications coming from outside our world.

articles.title_orig: A desert stirs to life: Chile's Atacama erupts in its biggest floral display in decades
articles.title_zh: A desert stirs to life: Chile's Atacama erupts in its biggest floral display in decades
articles.content_orig:
A field of colorful wildflowers blankets the Atacama Desert in northern Chile, transforming the world's driest non-polar desert into a vibrant landscape during the rare flowering desert phenomenon, known locally as the Desierto Florido, or Desert Bloom. Tamara Merino for NPR hide caption
COPIAPÓ, Chile — A vast swathe of Chile's Atacama Desert is now a patchwork of pinks, yellows, lilacs and purples stretching across the craggy desert floor as far as the eye can see.
This winter, heavy rains brought by the El Niño super cycle caused flash floods in the Atacama Desert, with some areas receiving the heaviest rainfall since records began in the 1950s.
Floodwaters in July and August destroyed or damaged dozens of homes,  forcing hundreds of people to evacuate.
A field of wildflowers blooms across Chile's Atacama Desert during the rare flowering phenomenon known as Desierto Florido, or Desert Bloom, triggered by unusually heavy rainfall that awakens dormant seeds. The brief blooms transform the world's driest nonpolar desert into a landscape of pink, purple, yellow and white. Huasco, Chile, Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026. Tamara Merino for NPR hide caption
But the floral bloom that followed has been the largest and most colorful in 30 years — and perhaps ever.
The rainwater penetrated deeper into the parched ground than it has in decades, allowing millions of seeds, bulbs and tubers to sprout above the surface. Many had lain dormant for decades under the sand.
More than 200 species are in flower. A month ago, the first plants to emerge created a pale-yellow haze. This was followed by a soft purple hue as other bulbs germinated. Now, almost every indentation and crevice in the desert is streaked with color.
Scientists studying the phenomenon say there are patches of desert in bloom where flowers have never previously been recorded, suggesting that bulbs have remained dormant there since before the phenomenon was first studied in detail in 1997.
Moisés Grimberg has served as the administrator of Llanos de Challe National Park for the past three years and has worked in protected area management for 18 years. His work focuses on protecting the flora, fauna, and fragile ecosystems of the coastal desert near Huasco, Chile, while also managing the influx of tourists during the rare flowering desert phenomenon, known locally as the Desierto Florido. Huasco, Chile, on Monday October 19, 2026. Tamara Merino for NPR. Tamera Merino for NPR hide caption
"This is a natural seed bank, a dormant archive that becomes a living one with the rains," says Moisés Grimberg, the administrator of Llanos de Challe National Park.
"But it's a race against time — this brief biological window allows these species to complete their life cycle, which lasts roughly two to three months."
Llanos de Challe is a 113,000-acre national park along the arid coastline, where waves lap at pristine white sand beaches.
Grimberg says the park normally receives about 10,000 visitors a year. But with the desert in bloom, 15,000 tourists have visited over the last few weeks alone.
Across the desert, the roads are lined with tourists' cars. According to Chile's national tourism board, the region is expected to see around 300,000 overnight trips during the two months the desert is in bloom.
Among the star attractions are the nectar-filled, crimson flowers of the garra de león, with their long tails of flame-like green leaves. This endemic flower is coaxed out of dormancy by the rains and grows along just a few miles of this stretch of coastline in the Atacama Desert — nowhere else in the world.
A Garra de León flower blooms in the Atacama Desert of northern Chile during the rare flowering desert phenomenon, known locally as the Desierto Florido. This striking native flower is known for its vibrant red petals and is one of the region's rare and emblematic desert species. Canto del Agua, Chile, on Tuesday October 20, 2026. Tamara Merino for NPR. Tamera Merino for NPR hide caption
This bloom occurs every few years in what is the driest nonpolar desert on Earth. But scientists say the phenomenon is becoming more frequent as changes in the climate bring unseasonal rains.
The phenomenon gives rise to a thriving, transient ecosystem, with insects hatching and attracting lizards and bats, as well as larger mammals such as the guanaco.
A guanaco stands amid a carpet of Malvilla and Pata de Guanaco wildflowers during the rare flowering desert phenomenon, known locally as the Desierto Florido, in the Atacama Desert of northern Chile. Canto del Agua, Chile, on Tuesday October 20, 2026. Tamara Merino for NPR hide caption
Biologists from INIA, Chile's national seed bank, are collecting specimens to analyze in their laboratory before the brief flowering season ends.
"It's very exciting," said Ana Sandoval as she delicately shook seeds free from their casings to take back to INIA's taxonomist at its base in northern Chile.
"It's as if the desert is awakening. Sometimes people think it's an empty, arid place, devoid of life, but actually our desert is just waiting for the right conditions, and any precipitation, to awaken it."
The seed bank wants to preserve the genetic material and unique adaptations each plant has developed to survive the extreme, arid conditions.
Sandoval points out different ways plants harvest water as she walks. Some leaves are covered in fine hairs; others have a thick waxy cuticle.
A national park dedicated to the desert bloom was created in June 2023 to protect a 141,000-acre area where flowers spring up every few years. Now local authorities want to go further.
A cactus, which survives year-round despite the desert's extreme temperatures, stands amid a carpet of Malvilla and Pata de Guanaco wildflowers during the rare flowering desert phenomenon, known locally as the Desierto Florido, in the Atacama Desert of northern Chile. Canto del Agua, Chile. Tamara Merino for NPR hide caption
Miguel Vargas, the governor of the Atacama region, is beginning the process of seeking UNESCO World Heritage recognition for the desert bloom phenomenon.
"This represents a tremendous opportunity to strengthen special interest tourism and diversify our regional economy, which is currently heavily reliant on mining," he said. "Receiving UNESCO recognition would put the Atacama region on the world stage."
A couple of tourists visits the Atacama Desert during the rare flowering desert phenomenon, known locally as the Desierto Florido, in northern Chile. Huasco, Chile, on Monday October 19, 2026. Tamara Merino for NPR hide caption
Vargas hopes this will become Chile's eighth World Heritage site within a couple of years.
This year, the bloom is projected to last until mid-November.
As the flowers begin to fade, scientists will be left with two tantalising questions: was this the Atacama Desert's largest flowering event on record, and might closer examination reveal any previously unknown species among the millions of plants?

articles.title_orig: AI stocks like Nvidia, Micron, and Sandisk have been blown up, but keep this in mind
articles.title_zh: AI stocks like Nvidia, Micron, and Sandisk have been blown up, but keep this in mind
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
I come to you today as a humble servant of the business and investing world with both good and bad news.
First, the sprinkles of good news, because I think we can agree we need something uplifting after watching the market get torched, blown up, and shredded to pieces in the aftermath of the blue wave .
Nothing changes in D.C. overnight, if at all. Companies' fundamentals are what will drive their stock prices in the long term. I don't think the fundamentals of companies have been destroyed this week, at least not to the extent that would warrant some of the sell-offs we witnessed.
A Hut 8 ( HUT ) data center build-out isn't getting a work order stoppage today that will derail the fourth quarter numbers. Dems aren't carting off AI data center C-suites to jail and sending their companies into bankruptcy.
Texas governor-elect Hinojosa isn't sending construction crews to data centers under an order to tear them all down and turn the land into parks. Elon Musk's SpaceX ( SPCX ) — based in Texas — is still operational this weekend, from what I can tell. Musk is still on pace to churn out Tesla ( TSLA ) robotaxis and robots in large numbers in 2027.
AMD ( AMD ) didn't offer a huge 2027 outlook this week on its earnings call because it fears a blue wave stopping its CPU momentum in its tracks.
In fact, AMD CEO Lisa Su told me the demand she is seeing is off the charts !
Hilton ( HLT ) CEO Chris Nassetta is so confident in his business trends that he told me this week he felt compelled to share directional guidance for 2027 with investors. Nassetta normally doesn't share these types of year-ahead specifics.
"Here's the reality. Our political system has been built pretty well," Nassetta said on Sozzi Unleashed . "Our founders did a pretty good job of creating a resilient system. We always figure it out. We'll figure it out this time. The reality is, in the next two or three years, I don't see any real dramatic impact as a result of the last couple days."
Nassetta is going on year 20 as CEO of Hilton, an almost unheard-of run in the C-suite. I don't think you get to log 20 years as Hilton CEO if you are wrong on a lot of stuff — and I think Chris makes a valid point on the political winds that are always blowing.
Now the bad news — and it's short and to the point.
We can no longer believe earnings estimates for 2027 and 2028. While in one breath I'm telling you corporate fundamentals haven't been destroyed this week, in the other breath I acknowledge they have taken a minor hit.
Data center projects won't come to a screeching halt in the US. It will just take a higher bar to get them built. And it will be costlier to get the deals done.
This was a surprise factor to the earnings estimates for the AI ecosystem, and that's what the market is adjusting to.
Should the selling in markets persist, it could be a surprise factor to the industrial companies supporting the AI boom — for example, Caterpillar ( CAT ) dump trucks. And from there, we get into the economic damage from a more restricted AI boom.
I am making a lot of assumptions here.
But will leave you with this: The world didn't end this week.
This is not the dot-com bust.
This is an adjustment period, and soon it'll be a period where you can no longer ignore the historically cheap valuations on names like Nvidia ( NVDA ), Micron, and Sandisk.

articles.title_orig: Canary Islands demand urgent government action amid surge in migrant arrivals
articles.title_zh: Canary Islands demand urgent government action amid surge in migrant arrivals
articles.content_orig:
El Hierro has declared a social emergency due to migratory pressure and, in parallel, the president of Vox, Santiago Abascal, has accused the president of the Government, Pedro Sánchez, and the Canary Islands Executive of wanting to "quickly distribute" migrants arriving on the island throughout Spain.
The far-right leader wrote this Saturday on X that the island is experiencing "another invasion" and assured that 8,000 people have arrived in a territory of 12,000 inhabitants. The statement is part of his political attack, but it does not alter the central fact: the Hierro Cabildo activated an extraordinary institutional response this Friday to a crisis that continues to accumulate arrivals.
Alpidio Armas, president of the Cabildo of El Hierro, formalized the social emergency and the need for collaboration with higher institutions by decree. According to the island institution, the situation has worsened in recent days and is putting pressure on human and care resources included in the care protocol.
In the last five days alone, the Cabildo counted more than 3,000 people aboard about thirty cayucos. The figure raises the total number of arrivals registered in the last five weeks to more than 8,000 , a volume that, according to the island corporation, exceeds the island's capacity to respond on its own.
Armas defended that the decision seeks to provide a response coordinated with the rest of the institutions , because, in his words, "El Hierro cannot face this alone." He also warned that the objective is to prevent the care protocol from "being overwhelmed or broken."
The decree requests the Government of the Canary Islands and the State to incorporate more human resources and a rotation that allows the teams working on the front line to rest. The demand extends to Maritime Rescue, the Canary Islands Health Service, the State Security Forces and Corps, the Red Cross and other NGOs involved in assisting migrants.
While Abascal insists on his accusation against the Government, the island institution keeps its focus on the operational management of the emergency. For now, the next step involves the response of the administrations to the request for reinforcement made by El Hierro.

articles.title_orig: DoorDash Shareholders Aren’t Convinced the Company Can Take On Amazon
articles.title_zh: DoorDash Shareholders Aren’t Convinced the Company Can Take On Amazon
articles.content_orig:
Last week, the news became official: DoorDash acquired Instacart for $17 billion.
Earlier in the week, when the deal was still a well-sourced rumor, Needham, an investment bank, put out a note regarding the deal. Needham’s working theory was that the deal is about combining the two advertising businesses. Everything else is logistics.
So what does this deal actually mean for commerce media?
The easy read is that a delivery app is buying another delivery app. Actually, DoorDash is buying a revenue mix it has never managed to build for itself. Not for lack of trying. DoorDash bought ad-tech company Symbiosys for $175 million in 2025 to take its ads beyond its own app, and it has spent years pushing into grocery and retail.
Buying Instacart is DoorDash’s admission that building on its own wasn’t getting there fast enough.
Here is the arithmetic. Instacart’s advertising and other revenue was $297 million in the second quarter, 28.5% of everything it earned. Call it more than a quarter of the company. DoorDash passed a $1 billion run rate in ads two years ago and hasn’t broken the number out since. By my count, that’s around 10% of its revenue.
Both companies have billion-dollar ad businesses. Only one of them is an ad business.
That matters because delivery is a hard business and advertising is a highly profitable one. According to Wedbush , a financial securities firm, Instacart brings more than grocery drop-offs; it brings a marketplace across many grocers, plus an ad business brands pay to rank higher in search.
Delivery is low margin, and ads are high margin. Ads lift what the platform earns per order without charging the customer more. That is the beauty of a blended P&L.
How did Instacart end up setting the bar? It became an ads business because the grocers couldn’t deliver what they had promised brands.
Retail media was pitched as performance media for commerce. Ads at the point of conversion, closed loop, every dollar accounted for. What brands got from most grocers was run-of-site advertising with a sales report attached.
Some grocers built serious networks, such as Kroger Precision Marketing and Albertsons Media Collective. But even the good ones could only reach one retailer’s shoppers, and that left brands stitching together a dozen buys to cover a category.
Instacart could do something the grocers couldn’t. Because it sat on top of the last mile, it could bundle baskets and get hyper-specific across hundreds of retailers in one buy. A brand didn’t have to negotiate with Kroger, then Costco, then Publix. It bought the category once.
That’s the Uber model – a network of independent operators behind one front door – applied to grocery. (Not so coincidentally, Uber was also reportedly in the mix to acquire Instacart, but it backed out.)
Together, DoorDash and Instacart reach across occasions no one else covers in one place. DoorDash’s share of US delivery spending has grown from 44% to 59% over five years, while Instacart’s fell from 26% to 18% . Combined, a CPG brand could find the same household ordering dinner on DoorDash on Tuesday and groceries on Instacart on Saturday, across restaurants, grocery and convenience in a single buy.
But Instacart has differentiators that could prove to be worth its $17 billion price tag. Instacart is not reliant on individual grocery retailers, because it has direct relationships with consumers. Consumers opt in to sharing loyalty card data with Instacart for rewards at the grocer, and Instacart carries that opt-in. Plus, Instacart operates its own planogram model, so it decides how prominently it features products based on its own brand deals.
All of those factors make Instacart a true commerce media business. And Instacart’s direct relationships with consumers and brands can’t be easily disrupted by a grocer deciding to launch its own retail media platform.
Meanwhile, DoorDash built its relationships directly with restaurants. So Instacart’s relationships with grocers are truly additive.
Now, here’s the uncomfortable part: attribution.
Instacart nailed attribution on its own app. It has a 14-day window, basket-level reporting, a clean room since January and MRC accreditation for its impressions and clicks. What it never nailed is attribution to the retailer’s total sales, which is what the grocers promised in the first place.
Instacart sees the Instacart basket. Most grocery still happens in a store, and that halo is modeled, not measured. Brands kept spending anyway. They pay for the basket, not the proof. What is interesting is that the burden of proof shifted to the retailer rather than Instacart. Instacart can prove what happens in its own basket. So when a brand asks what its spend did in the store, the retailer is the one left without an answer.
There’s a bigger point here for commerce media. We’ve spent five years calling it an emerging channel, the thing on the test budget. It has just been priced as a scaled business asset, with closed-loop measurement on its own basket and modeling to show brands its impact in-store.
A public company just paid $17 billion, about a 30% premium, largely for an ad business built on shopper data. And the analysts covering the deal are valuing that ad business, not the drivers.
Commerce media is no longer just a line in the marketing plan; it is a line in the acquisition model.
“ Data-Driven Thinking ” is written by members of the media community and contains fresh ideas on the digital revolution in media.
Follow Kristina Kaganer , Auxbow and AdExchanger on LinkedIn.
Why the midterms may not spell doom for ad tech consolidation. Plus, how sports leagues are putting ad revenue before player safety.
Agentic media buying is the No. 1 topic du jour in ad tech discussion circles. But how does agentic buying even work when it comes to buying TV and streaming ads? And how does that workflow differ from programmatic? The startup Swivel aims to address those questions.
AppLovin is growing at a blistering pace, but Wall Street investors remain cautious about the business.
High-end ad blockers mimic some of the same behavior as bot traffic. So WiseGuyGaming repurposed the tools it was already using to identify bots to reveal its ad-blocking audience as well.
Criteo has weathered considerable storms in its day, including a painful moment in March 2020 when its market cap bottomed out below $500 million. Can it pull off yet another turnaround?
Disaffection and outright anger toward US sports institutions run deeper than logo-cluttered fields. Leagues and teams are sacrificing player safety and fan enjoyment for marketing dollars.

articles.title_orig: New Zealand dairy giant Fonterra speeds up China innovation
articles.title_zh: New Zealand dairy giant Fonterra speeds up China innovation
articles.content_orig:
Fonterra Co-operative Group Ltd is accelerating product development with Chinese customers as the New Zealand dairy giant seeks to capture growing demand for protein-rich foods and dairy products tailored to local tastes.
The company is leveraging its six application centers in China to help bakeries, beverage chains and food manufacturers bring new products to market faster, supported by investments in production capacity in New Zealand, CEO Richard Allen said in an interview during the China International Import Expo in Shanghai.
"We know how fast the China market moves and how quickly trends change," Allen said. "Alongside our customers, we can work with them to create new products with new selling points."
A recent visit to Chengdu, Sichuan province, highlighted how much the market had evolved since he worked in China's foodservice sector many years ago.
Allen said dairy products had become more prominent in bakeries, supermarkets and membership stores, with a growing number of products emphasizing their protein content.
Chinese food and beverage brands are also increasingly highlighting the grass-fed origins of New Zealand dairy ingredients to differentiate their products and strengthen their premium positioning.
However, turning those attributes into sales requires products that deliver both quality and value.
Fonterra works with customers to select ingredients that meet nutritional and taste requirements while keeping costs affordable for consumers and commercially viable for producers, Allen said.
"You've got to have nutrition, but it also has to taste good," he said.
Its six application centers in China bring together chefs, marketing specialists and sales teams to develop products suited to local and regional tastes.
For one bakery customer, Fonterra explored incorporating Sichuan's signature mala, or spicy and numbing, flavors into baked goods. Allen also cited the pairing of Anchor butter with pineapple buns as an example of how dairy ingredients can be incorporated into established local food traditions.
"By being on the ground, close to our customers, to their consumers, it allows us to work every day with our customers on developing new products very quickly," he said.
China is also becoming a source of product innovation for Fonterra's operations elsewhere in Asia.
Dairy-topped tea drinks developed in China, for example, have created opportunities among the company's foodservice customers in Southeast Asia, Allen said.
Meanwhile, the overseas expansion of Chinese restaurant and beverage chains is opening another avenue for growth.
As these brands enter international markets, they increasingly seek consistent supplies of familiar ingredients to maintain product quality and taste across their global operations.
Fonterra is supporting Chinese customers expanding into Southeast Asia, the United States, Europe, Australia and New Zealand, drawing on its international supply network and foodservice expertise.
"Not only can we support our local customers in other markets, but we can support Chinese brands in accessing other markets," Allen said.
The strategy builds on Fonterra's established ingredients and foodservice businesses in China, where the cooperative has operated for nearly five decades.
Allen described China as one of Fonterra's cornerstone markets, with demand for dairy ingredients and nutritional products continuing to create opportunities for long-term growth.
To support that demand, Fonterra is investing NZ$150 million ($87 million) to expand ultra-high-temperature cream production at its Edendale facility in New Zealand.
The additional capacity will serve customers in China and other markets, complementing investments in local application centers and culinary, marketing and sales teams.
The expansion comes as Fonterra reported stronger financial results for the year ended July 2026. The cooperative posted revenue of NZ$27 billion and total group operating profit of NZ$3.4 billion in results released on Sept 24.
Fonterra has also announced an additional NZ$1 billion investment over three years to expand its protein manufacturing network in New Zealand's South Island and improve environmental performance.
In China, Allen sees further opportunities in protein-rich products. During his visits to Chinese supermarkets, he was struck by the growing number of products promoting their protein content.
"For us, being agile and moving fast, and ensuring our customers are agile and moving fast, is about being close to the market and really understanding what's happening," Allen said.

China has confirmed that it is discussing a historic meeting of Xi Jinping , Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump .
Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said at a press briefing this week that Beijing was “in communication with relevant parties regarding a meeting between the three heads of state” .
The three-leader gathering could take place this month on the sidelines of a regional summit in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen .
It would be historic if the meeting were to happen, but experts argued the leaders of China, Russia and the US were unlikely to discuss anything substantive because their interests were at odds. They would gather for a photo, the experts said, with China carefully choreographing the meeting .
“I think it will happen. The question is the format and the content,” Sun Yun, director of the Stimson Centre’s China programme, said. “China wants the image but not the costs.”
Beijing is hosting this year’s summit of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, a 21-member grouping that includes the US and Russia, this month.
Mr Trump is expected to travel to Shenzhen and meet the Chinese leader for the third time this year, maintaining a fragile trade truce that is set to expire in January.
In a sign that tensions persist, American trade representative Jamieson Greer urged China during a video call with vice premier He Lifeng on Friday to take “concrete actions to fully implement its past commitments, particularly as they relate to agricultural purchases, rare earths, and critical minerals”.
Chinese news agency Xinhua reported on Saturday that the two sides had constructive exchanges and that Beijing expressed concerns about Washington’s restrictive economic and trade measures against it.
Mr Trump previously said that he would be interested in meeting Mr Xi and Mr Putin to discuss nuclear arms controls, though Mr Putin was focused on talking about the Ukraine war without Kyiv at the table.
“Putin has the most to gain from a leaders’ trilateral and the Russians are clearly behind the push for a meeting, which would be a diplomatic coup,” said Danny Russel, a former senior US State Department official who served in former president Barack Obama ’s administration.
Mr Trump, with his “crush on authoritarian strongmen", would love the meeting, though he clearly had been warned by his advisers to steer clear of Ukraine as a topic of the discussions, said Mr Russel.
Ms Sun of the Stimson Centre said Russia would likely use the summit to nudge China and the US closer to Moscow's positions on Ukraine, while “China will have to manage Russian manipulation”.
China also would not engage in talks on arms controls or discussions about Ukraine or Iran, other than its diplomatic refrain that peace was important and wars should end, Ms Sun said.
Beijing's biggest challenge might be the perception. The summit “should not be equated to three great powers dividing up the world”, she said.
The meeting might amount to no more than a photo opportunity that would allow Mr Putin to be seen next to American and Chinese leaders, Craig Singleton, senior director of the China programme at the Foundation for Defence of Democracies, said.
“But these photo opportunities have diminishing diplomatic returns,” Mr Singleton said. “The spectacle may be historic without producing anything particularly consequential.”

articles.title_orig: Putin Seizes Three More Japan Tobacco Businesses, Bringing Takeover to $3.7 Billion
articles.title_zh: Putin Seizes Three More Japan Tobacco Businesses, Bringing Takeover to $3.7 Billion
articles.content_orig:
Russian leader Vladimir Putin has placed three additional subsidiaries of Japan Tobacco International (JTI) under Russian-appointed management, expanding Moscow’s takeover of the Japanese tobacco giant’s operations to seven companies, with the affected assets valued at up to $3.7 billion.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to The Moscow Times on November 7, the latest presidential decree transferred control of JTI Russia, Pereslavl-Tabak, and JTI Innovative Products to the Russian company Industrial Assets.
The decision follows a separate decree issued on November 5 that placed four JTI manufacturing and tobacco-related businesses under the same management structure.
Bloomberg reported that the newly affected companies include a holding entity, a cigarette distribution business, and an importer of electronic tobacco products and heated tobacco systems.
The earlier takeover covered Petro, JTI Donskoy Tabak, Kres Neva, and JTI Yelets, which collectively employ approximately 4,000 people. According to The Moscow Times, Russian industry analysts estimate the combined value of the affected assets at 250 billion to 300 billion rubles, or approximately $3.1 billion to $3.7 billion.
Industrial Assets was established in September 2026. Russian corporate records identify Sergei Dremov, a former member of the State Council of Russian-occupied Crimea, as one of its founders. His biography indicates that he served in Russian state security agencies between 2000 and 2016.
JTI has operated in Russia since 1999 and previously controlled up to 40% of the country’s cigarette market, selling brands including Winston, Camel, Sobranie, and LD. JTI has operated in Russia since 1999 and previously controlled up to 40% of the country’s cigarette market, selling brands including Winston, Camel, Sobranie, and LD.
Despite Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the company remained in the country, suspending new investments before deciding in 2023 to continue operations.
The expanded takeover follows Japan’s formal protest over Moscow’s initial decision. On November 6, Tokyo demanded that Russia reverse the measure, while Japan’s Foreign Ministry raised the issue with Russian Ambassador Nikolay Nozdrev.

articles.title_orig: Missile strikes multi-story Aramco building in Riyadh’s financial district, witnesses say
articles.title_zh: Missile strikes multi-story Aramco building in Riyadh’s financial district, witnesses say
articles.content_orig:
A building belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco in the financial district in the capital Riyadh has been damaged in a missile attack.
The strike in King Abdullah Financial District was reported after Saudi Civil Defense issued ‌an early-warning ⁠alert of a potential threat to the city.
Video circulating on social media and verified by CNN shows damage to upper floors of the Aramco building, with windows seen blown out. But Saudi authorities said the impact was minimal.
“An administrative building belonging to Saudi Aramco in Riyadh was subjected to an attempted attack,” on Sunday, according to the official Saudi news agency, citing a source at the Saudi Energy Ministry.
“The incident resulted in falling shrapnel that caused minor damage to the building, with no injuries or fatalities reported,” the agency reported.
However, one witness said they saw ambulances heading to the area.
CNN has reached out to the Information Ministry by email for further details.
The Houthis, who have fired missiles and drones towards multiple targets across Saudi Arabia over the last three months, have not claimed responsibility.
Multiple loud booms were ⁠heard in the Saudi capital ⁠Riyadh early Sunday.
The Saudi led coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed two cruise missiles in Riyadh and the southern region. Coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki wrote in a post on X that air defenses also “intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the terrorist Houthi militia towards Riyadh.”
The missile attacks on Riyadh came a day after Yemen’s Houthi-run health ministry said Saudi airstrikes had ‌killed ‌at least ​33 ​people near the capital Sanaa, including women and children.
“We will punish the Saudi regime for its crimes against the Yemeni people,” said Mahdi al-Mashat, a senior Houthi official, on Saturday.
Last month, 13 people were killed in one missile strike on Riyadh’s international airport, and several more died in other strikes on the airport.
The Houthis have said they will continue firing missiles and drones against Saudi Arabia so long as the Kingdom carries out airstrikes against the parts of Yemen they control and enforces a blockade against its territory.
Saudi Arabia spent $83 billion on defense last year, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, putting it firmly among the top ten military spenders worldwide. It has acquired US fighter jets as well as Patriot and THAAD air defense systems, and a range of advanced weaponry from France and the United Kingdom.
But the Saudis have a lot to defend: a country roughly one-fifth the size of the US, with threats on three sides - from Iran , Iranian-backed militias in Iraq, and the Houthis.
Iran’s hardliners see a weakened Trump – and want more to end the war
The Saudis are intercepting many of the missiles and drones fired by the Houthis. But some get through. The defense ministry faces difficult choices in distributing the existing systems with so many installations vulnerable to attack.
The Houthis have learned to combine ballistic and cruise missiles with long-range drones to overwhelm Saudi defenses, according to analysts.
In Yemen, the Saudi-backed coalition is trying to prevent the Houthis from advancing further south towards the port of Aden, which is held by the internationally-recognized government.
The Houthis have frequently targeted Aden’s airport with missiles in recent weeks, after taking a stretch of Yemen’s Red Sea coast in September.
Hostilities between the Houthis, who are backed by Iran, and Saudi Arabia reignited in July, shattering a 2022 UN-brokered ceasefire that had largely halted fighting ⁠between the ‌two sides.

articles.title_orig: Israel's president taps opposition candidate, not Netanyahu, to form a government
articles.title_zh: Israel's president taps opposition candidate, not Netanyahu, to form a government
articles.content_orig:
Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar ("Straight") party, waves an Israeli flag onstage last month in Tel Aviv following the release of the first exit poll results in Israel's general election. Ariel Schalit/AP hide caption
Israel's president has tapped Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's main political rival, Gadi Eisenkot, to try to form the next government. It's a setback for Netanyahu, whose party won the most seats but failed to secure a parliamentary majority.
Netanyahu's Likud party won 27 seats in last month's election, six more than Eisenkot's Yashar party. But neither secured enough support to command a majority in Israel's 120-seat parliament.
President Isaac Herzog will formally give Eisenkot the mandate at 5 p.m. local time on Sunday. Herzog made the decision after parties representing most of the members of Israel's parliament recommended Eisenkot to try forming a governing coalition.
Eisenkot is a former chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces, serving as the country's top military commander from 2015 to 2019. A veteran of several military campaigns, he later joined Netanyahu's emergency war cabinet following the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attacks on Israel, but left the following year, accusing Netanyahu of failing to make progress toward ending the Gaza war and securing the release of hostages.
Eisenkot lost his son, Gal, a reservist killed in Gaza, as well as two nephews during the war.
He leads the center-right Yashar party, which he founded on an anti-corruption and government reform platform. He will now have 28 days to put together a coalition government, with a possible 14-day extension.
That gives him up to six weeks to negotiate with rival parties and secure the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority.
The coalition building promises to be a tough task and could include strange bedfellows: from ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties to Arab-led parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel — who make up about 20% of Israel and had a record turnout in these elections.
They could now potentially be the kingmakers. But both Eisenkot and Netanyahu ruled out working with them before the elections. Now there's some public pressure on Eisenkot to change his mind, and on Saturday Netanyahu issued a video warning against that.
He said it would be partnering with what he called Hamas supporters and "those who oppose Judaism." Eisenkot responded, calling Netanyahu's video hysterical.
If Eisenkot fails, Herzog can give another lawmaker a chance to form a government. If those efforts also fail, Israel could face another election. Netanyahu would remain caretaker prime minister in the meantime.

articles.title_orig: China's solar push reshapes life on Tibet's high plateau
articles.title_zh: China's solar push reshapes life on Tibet's high plateau
articles.content_orig:
GONGHE, China – Life has become unexpectedly easier and more lucrative for some shepherds on the world’s highest plateau, after China began carpeting the area with solar panels in a drive to diversify its energy mix.
“It has made grazing much easier for us,” said Li Yonglin, 25, one of those allowed to freely graze their sheep in a fenced solar park in Gonghe, a county in the northwestern province of Qinghai.
“In the morning, we simply open the gate to the sheep pen and don’t really need to look after them. They come back on their own in the evening, and we just pen them up.”
Li estimated the new approach had boosted his earnings to between 50,000 yuan and 60,000 yuan ($7,496.14 and $8,995.37) from 10,000 yuan to 20,000 yuan when he followed the old way.
By July this year, state media said, 6,330 households in five townships had benefited from 56 grazing sites in Hainan, a culturally Tibetan area that encompasses Gonghe, but did not disclose how many got grazing access.
Such early signs suggest China’s projects sprawling over hundreds of acres on the vast Qinghai-Tibet plateau are boosting incomes for some, though researchers and others warn they are also eroding traditional ways of life.
One study estimated the region, sometimes called “the roof of the world,“ where nomadic communities have grazed livestock for millennia, holds almost half of China’s solar energy potential, making it a focal point for renewable energy efforts.
Solar overtook coal in July as the country’s biggest source of installed power capacity, and authorities plan to expand wind and solar power generation by a further 53% in the next five years.
The complex Li visits, sprawling over 148,000 acres (60,000 hectares), uses grazing sheep to reduce mowing costs, said Cao Jun, a safety supervisor for a State Power Investment Corporation project in Hainan.
It leads to a “win-win situation,“ he said, with power generated by the plant sent nationwide to cities such as Beijing, the capital and the commercial hub of Shanghai.
But the integration of livestock and solar infrastructure has not been universally welcomed.
Researchers say solar projects are transforming life on the plateau, where thousands of Tibetan nomads were resettled into rural townships in the early 2000s as the government sought to reverse ecological degradation.
“You can find some places (to graze) around the solar panels, but these are not suitable for nomads and shepherds to hold their livelihood,” said researcher Tsewang Dorji at the Tibet Policy Institute, a think tank of the Tibetan government-in-exile, in India’s hill town of Dharamsala.
Plateau dwellers get little say in the conversion of pastures to solar power projects, said one researcher studying environmental conservation and new energy infrastructure there.
Such installations fragment once-open grazing lands, making herders’ task of watching over livestock harder, added the researcher, who sought anonymity in order to protect collaborators.
Sheep from 16 households were allowed to graze in a solar park for part of the year, the government in Gonghe said in 2024.
A small number of nomads were “tokenistically employed to graze sheep” but goats and yaks were generally excluded, said Mandie McKeown, advocacy director at the environmental charity Foundation for Gaia, which is based in Britain.
Evidence shows “This isn’t pastoralism as it’s traditionally been practiced,” McKeown said.
Wind rattling through solar farm posts and wires produced “persistent and unsettling” sounds that disturbed both people and animals, anthropology researcher Sanggay Tashi at the University of Colorado Boulder said in an article in June, citing people in Qinghai.
Online government records in 2017 showed one undated complaint that Gonghe’s photovoltaic power stations had damaged grasslands, leaving sheep and cattle little grass to eat.
The records, which cited Hainan as the administrative region for the case without identifying the aggrieved person, said an investigation found no truth in the accusation, while adding that grazing was not permitted in the area.
Authorities in Qinghai did not respond to requests for comment.
Not everyone in Gonghe is complaining, though.
“Life has changed tremendously,” said another shepherd, Wen Yujun, who now finds himself able to manage a herd of 700 to 800 largely on his own.
“I never could have imagined it before,” added the 43-year-old, who estimated his annual income had risen eightfold to about 80,000 yuan.

articles.title_orig: Russia races to build rival to Elon Musk’s Starlink
articles.title_zh: Russia races to build rival to Elon Musk’s Starlink
articles.content_orig:
Experts on Russia's Security Council warned Friday that Russia needs to urgently expand its homegrown equivalent to Starlink, warning that Elon Musk's satellite network could be used to destabilize countries throughout the world.
In a statement cited by state media, the Security Council said "it is necessary to rapidly scale up the mass production of communications satellites and terminal equipment," referring to Russia's Rassvet low-Earth orbit satellite network.
Digital Development Minister Maksut Shadayev told President Vladimir Putin last month that Russia has so far launched just over 30 satellites as part of Rassvet. In comparison, Starlink has more than 10,000 active satellites.
On Friday, Russia's Security Council held a meeting of its expert council to discuss issues related to information security and internet access.
"During the meeting, the main risks and threats posed by the use of Western space-based communications systems over the territory of sovereign states to destabilize the socio-political situation were highlighted," it said in its statement.
"This applies, first and foremost, to the widely used satellite communications services Starlink and OneWeb," it added.
Just days ago, Putin praised Elon Musk as a "real genius" for developing Starlink. Ukraine's army has used the military version of the satellite internet network throughout the war with Russia for drone operations and battlefield communications.
Dmitry Medvedev, who serves as deputy chairman of Russia's Security Council, criticized Musk on Friday for allowing Ukraine to use Starlink.
Ukraine said that Russia is already employing its new Rassvet satellite network for military communications in Ukraine.

articles.title_orig: Crypto industry braces for reckoning over Trump ties
articles.title_zh: Crypto industry braces for reckoning over Trump ties
articles.content_orig:
This article was contributed by Binance
The second Trump term has put cryptocurrencies on center stage, not only as a policy priority but as a source of real income for the president himself.
The country is suddenly talking about Bitcoin reserves, government-backed stockpiles and Trump’s crypto businesses generating more revenue than his real estate empire. The market is responding in ways not seen before. As of September 25, 2026, the Bitcoin to USD rate was $83,376.06, according to data from Binance. And Washington might have as much influence over the price as basic supply and demand.
In March 2025, Trump signed an executive order creating a Strategic Bitcoin Reserve. This pool was initially filled with Bitcoin already in government hands, seized during various criminal and civil forfeiture cases, according to an official statement from the White House. Alongside that, there’s a Digital Asset Stockpile for other coins. The plan is simple enough: Hold Bitcoin like the U.S. holds gold or oil, and make it a national reserve asset.
More than a year later, this reserve is still mostly for show. The administration keeps insisting that Congress needs to step in before things take off, and while a bill is expected to be reintroduced under a fresh name, so far it’s all been talk, according to Yahoo Finance. Early numbers suggested the government had about 200,000 BTC, though the U.S. Marshals Service isn’t so sure about that, according to CCN.
That Bitcoin reserve was just the warm-up. In July 2025, Trump greenlit the GENIUS Act, the first real federal framework for stablecoins backed by U.S. dollars. Now, payment stablecoins get official recognition: They’re neither securities nor commodities, finally cutting through years of confusion, according to a fact sheet from the White House.
Banks, asset managers and large corporations have shown renewed interest in stablecoins following the regulatory clarity. Regulated stablecoins are becoming a preferred tool for settling tokenized securities and on-chain payments, a shift that could open the door to significant new capital, according to Yahoo Finance and Investing.com. The Trump administration has also appointed crypto-friendly regulators across federal agencies. In May 2026, Trump signed another executive order requiring regulators to drop rules that kept banks from partnering with fintech and crypto companies, according to a fact sheet from the White House .
All these regulatory resets have supercharged the industry and Trump’s business interests. His 2025 financial disclosure, sent to the Office of Government Ethics and made public on June 30, 2026, shows digital assets as his top income stream. His companies pulled in nearly $800 million from World Liberty Financial, the crypto project he co-founded with his sons. That includes $520 million from token sales, and another $250 million by selling stakes in the venture. On top of that, Trump scored another $635 million through sales of the $TRUMP meme coin, which he launched just before returning to office. All this has been reported by Time and Reuters.
Sum it up, and Trump’s family crypto businesses brought in more than $1.4 billion in reported income for 2025. Reuters says crypto was the single biggest driver of his $2.2 billion in total disclosed earnings, beating out real estate and legal settlements combined. When he was called out for it, Trump told reporters, “You know why I’m profiting, because the stock market’s going up, everybody’s profiting,” according to Reuters. For context, his crypto income from the same venture in 2024 was about $57 million, so it grew more than tenfold in just one year, riding the wave of policy changes, according to BBC.
It’s not just empty promises. Companies in the sector have started making real moves thanks to regulatory clarity. Stablecoin issuers, payment platforms and crypto on/off ramp providers are citing the GENIUS Act as the reason they’re ramping up U.S. operations instead of dodging them, according to The Economic Times.
Banks that used to steer clear of crypto because of a 2022 FDIC directive can now roll out digital asset products that follow the rules, according to Legal500.
Dollar moves matter to Bitcoin buyers. The Press Banner’s money column on protecting your portfolio from a falling dollar covers the same concern that has drawn some investors toward Bitcoin during Trump’s second term.
Has the U.S. government bought more Bitcoin for its reserve?
No, not yet. The Strategic Bitcoin Reserve, created in March 2025, only includes Bitcoin seized through criminal and civil cases.
Does the GENIUS Act regulate Bitcoin itself?
No. The GENIUS Act is purely about U.S. dollar-backed stablecoins. It forces issuers to back their tokens one-to-one with cash and Treasury securities, and to publish monthly reserve reports.
How much has Bitcoin moved in September 2026 alone?
It ran from about $76,800 on September 2 to $83,376.06 on September 25, 2026, according to Binance.

articles.title_orig: Apple saves $2.7bn in taxes by booking profits in Singapore
articles.title_zh: Apple saves $2.7bn in taxes by booking profits in Singapore
articles.content_orig:
Apple's new annual report shows Singapore cut its tax bill by about $2.7 billion in fiscal 2026, more than Ireland. Why is the breakdown public only now?
Published 08.11.2026 11:10 3 min read
Apple Singapore tax savings reached about $2.7 billion in fiscal 2026, more than the roughly $2.6 billion the iPhone maker saved through Ireland, according to a Financial Times analysis of Apple's annual report published on Sunday, November 8, 2026. The FT estimates Apple booked up to $50 billion of profit in the city-state during the year that ended September 26.
The figures come from Apple's Form 10-K filed on November 3, which for the first time breaks down the company's tax bill country by country.
In the tax reconciliation of its fiscal 2026 annual report , Apple lists a $5.49 billion reduction from Singapore's lower tax rate, including incentives, measured against the 21% US federal rate. That benefit is partly offset by a $2.51 billion Singapore top-up tax and $311 million in other items, leaving a net saving of about $2.67 billion, or roughly €2.3 billion.
Ireland's line shows a $3.46 billion rate benefit minus $897 million in other items, a net of about $2.57 billion. Apple does not publish profit by country, so the "up to $50 billion" Singapore figure is the Financial Times' estimate , not a number from the filing.
Starting with its 2026 report, Apple adopted the US accounting standard ASU 2023-09, which requires companies to itemize large reconciling items by jurisdiction and disclose cash taxes paid by country. Until last year, Apple grouped its foreign tax effects together.
Singapore's top-up tax is the city-state's version of the global 15% minimum tax for groups with at least €750 million in revenue, which applies from financial years starting in 2025. It narrows the gap with the US rate but, as the filing shows, does not close it.
Apple reported $159.2 billion in pre-tax income for fiscal 2026, of which $95.5 billion was foreign, and a $27.06 billion tax provision. Its effective tax rate rose to 17.0% from 15.6% in fiscal 2025, which Apple attributes mainly to a higher rate on foreign earnings and US currency loss rules. In fiscal 2024 the rate was 24.1% because of a one-time $10.2 billion charge after the EU's top court ordered Apple to pay Ireland back taxes.
The filing came a day after Apple reported record fiscal 2026 revenue of $478.8 billion , up about 15% from a year earlier.
It also lands as European governments keep looking for new ways to tax Big Tech, from global minimum taxes to proposals such as the France internet tax on data traffic.
Nothing in the filing suggests Apple broke any rules, and the minimum tax is already cutting into the benefit. But the new country-level data shows that Singapore, not Ireland, is now the biggest single lever in Apple's tax bill, and that will draw attention from lawmakers who spent a decade focused on Cork.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine war briefing: Russia ramping up attacks to ‘pressure’ Kyiv at trilateral talks, Zelenskyy says
articles.title_zh: Ukraine war briefing: Russia ramping up attacks to ‘pressure’ Kyiv at trilateral talks, Zelenskyy says
articles.content_orig:
President urges US for support, saying ‘Ukraine must not be left to face this alone’ as barrage plunges cities into darkness. What we know on day 1,719
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused Russia of intensifying strikes across the country to put pressure on Kyiv at upcoming talks after an overnight barrage triggered power cuts as temperatures drop. “By intensifying its attacks on Ukraine and our infrastructure at this very moment, Russia is trying to additionally lay the groundwork for putting pressure on Ukraine’s position and that of its partners,” the Ukrainian president said. “Russia perceives diplomacy in its own peculiar way – as a form of aggression.”
Ukraine’s energy ministry said “a massive attack on a number of energy facilities” on Saturday had plunged five regions into darkness and significantly hampered electricity transmission in Kyiv and surrounding regions. Russia had throughout the night launched 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles, Zelenskyy said, among which were KN-23 missiles manufactured and supplied by North Korea.
The strikes came before a US-brokered trilateral meeting in Abu Dhabi scheduled for next week aimed at reviving stalled diplomatic efforts towards peace. Ukrainian officials are expected to sit down with Russian negotiators and US envoys on Tuesday and Wednesday for the first such talks in months. The diplomatic track has been stalled since February when Washington shifted attention to its war with Iran.
Zelenskyy also urged the US to increase its flagging aid to Ukraine. “Unfortunately, there is still a significant shortage of interceptors for Patriot systems, and the United States is in the best position to help address it,” he said.
Italy’s foreign minister, Antonio Tajani , on Saturday said he had been targeted by pro-Russian hackers over his backing for Ukraine . Tajani said in a post on X that “backing in a transparent way the freedom and independence of a sovereign state” had made him a target. Tajani said his personal data had been published on the dark web and that the hackers were seeking further information about him and his family and were ‌willing to pay for it.
The Italian prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, who has been one of the strongest backers of Ukraine among western leaders, expressed her support for Tajani and said the sale of confidential information relating to public officials was “a matter of serious concern”. Moscow has not commented ‌on the incident. ‌
France’s far-left presidential contender Jean-Luc Mélenchon said on Saturday that settling the Ukraine conflict could not be done by granting territorial concessions without consulting the people concerned . Melenchon, who polls suggest could reach the second round of next year’s presidential election, set out his France Unbowed party’s foreign policy positions at a rally just outside Paris.
Mélenchon has been criticised in the past for questioning the legitimacy of Zelenskyy. But in a campaign speech to thousands of supporters, he said an administration run by his party would take an active role in settling the war in Ukraine . Europe would have to play an active role in peace talks, he said. “We cannot accept that one could consider a peace with territorial concessions in Ukraine without asking the populations concerned if they agree or not to be on one side or other of the border,” he said. “It is for the people themselves to decide what they want,” he added.
A Ukrainian attack killed one person in Russia’s Belgorod region when a drone hit a private home in the town of Grayvoron, local officials said on Saturday. Russia’s defence ministry said its forces shot down 411 Ukrainian drones overnight over 10 Russian regions, including Belgorod. Drones were also destroyed over the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black and Azov seas, it said. Russian media outlets later reported that the Saratov Oil Refinery had been hit and shared images of plumes of smoke over the city.
